item.title: Byte-sized — Wednesday, 25 November
item.description:
Good morning, and welcome to Byte-sized for Wednesday the twenty-fifth of November. Six sections today, starting as always in Japan and the Asia Pacific.
Section one, Japan and Asia Pacific.
A quick note first: there was no Japan-specific story in today's newsletters, so this section looks across the wider region.
First, Australia moves to replace China in the Solomon Islands. Canberra is reportedly offering the Solomon Islands about six hundred and sixty-seven million dollars under a sweeping new security treaty, due to be signed today. It would replace the contentious security pact the Solomons signed with Beijing in twenty twenty-two, which alarmed Western capitals and set off the current race for influence in the Pacific. If it goes through, it is a clear strategic win for Australia, and a sign that the Pacific contest is now being fought with large cheques rather than speeches. Via International Intrigue.
Second, A I agents are now running real attacks in East Asia. Security researchers describe a China-linked group that pointed autonomous A I agents at East Asian universities for about forty-eight hours. The agents ran nearly a hundred and fifty actions against an exposed database server, tried more than thirty thousand password combinations on a G P U server, then found a flaw in an open-source medical imaging application and took full control of the machine within eleven minutes. In the same newsletter, the United States Justice Department moved to seize about one point one seven billion dollars in stablecoins linked to North Korea's Lazarus Group and October's six billion dollar Binance hack. For anyone running university or hospital infrastructure in the region, the lesson is that the time between a weakness being found and being used is collapsing. Via T L D R Information Security.
And third, Indonesia's president goes into bat for his stock market. Prabowo Subianto held direct talks, reportedly brokered by the American billionaire Ray Dalio, with the index provider M S C I, to try to head off a damaging downgrade of Indonesia's market status. A downgrade would force index-tracking funds to sell Indonesian shares. It is unusual for a head of state to negotiate with an index company personally, and it shows how much emerging Asian economies now depend on passive global capital. Via International Intrigue.
Now, over to A I and tech.
Section two, A I and tech.
First, the Nvidia story takes another turn. We covered Jensen Huang's reinstatement yesterday; the new detail is how it happened and what comes with it. President Trump says he personally lobbied Nvidia's board, which voted unanimously to bring Huang back just eleven days after he resigned, and the shares jumped more than thirty per cent, the largest single-day gain in value for any stock in history. Nvidia says it will set up a national security and export control committee and appoint a chief compliance officer, while independent directors keep investigating claims that Huang was targeted by foreign intelligence. Huang still faces a House hearing on the first of December, and the Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries has called the decision indefensible. Benedict Evans, writing just before the reversal, put the governance problem bluntly: the board was weighing a founder the company was built around against a record of affairs, a customer linked to chip smuggling, and repeated dishonesty to the board itself. Via The Rundown A I, T L D R A I and Benedict Evans.
Second, Meta's A I chief says superintelligence is arriving. Alexandr Wang published an essay arguing that the industry needs to take, in his words, meaningfully different actions from the path it is on. He pointed to Claude's role in the Riemann hypothesis proof as evidence that A I could soon speed up almost every field beyond what humans can follow, and said society should not accept a handover to A I. That is a striking shift in tone from Meta, whose boss Mark Zuckerberg has usually brushed off calls to slow down. Benedict Evans adds the sharper question: if machines produce proofs that are correct but run to a quarter of a million pages, what is that knowledge actually for if no one can understand it? Via The Rundown A I and Benedict Evans.
Third, coding agents move from writing code to shipping it. Anthropic has launched Claude Ship, a set of agents that review pull requests, push fixes, and check changes against a team's own approval rules before anything is merged. It is available on Team and Enterprise plans for code held on GitHub. Separately, Slack has started offering its Claude-powered Slackbot at a flat price per person rather than per use, pitching it as a way to stop companies rationing A I because they fear surprise bills. Both point the same way: the business model is shifting from selling a model to selling finished work at a predictable price. Via T L D R Founders and T L D R I T.
And fourth, OpenAI is paying local people to teach small businesses. Its new pilot, OpenWorks, pays tech-savvy people up to eight thousand dollars a month to sit with small business owners in twenty American cities, mostly in the Midwest and South, and help them use A I on a problem the owner chooses. Businesses get three months of ChatGPT Business free, and venture-backed and private equity-owned firms are excluded. It is a clever bit of distribution: a paid route into A I consulting for the helpers, and a pipeline of new business customers for OpenAI. Via The Rundown A I.
Now, over to startups and venture.
Section three, startups and venture.
First, the security industry consolidates in a very big way. CrowdStrike has agreed to buy Zscaler in an all-stock deal worth about forty-four billion dollars, a premium of roughly a third. Combining endpoint protection with Zscaler's zero-trust networking gives a business with more than ten billion dollars of annual recurring revenue, and CrowdStrike is pitching it as the control layer for securing A I agents. It comes as security firms report being so overwhelmed by A I-driven attacks that some are turning away new clients. Via T L D R I T and T L D R Information Security.
Second, Amazon buys an A I efficiency team for seven and a half billion dollars. Amazon has acquired the technology behind Decart's optimisation software, along with its founders and research team. The software helps A I models run efficiently on Nvidia, Google and Amazon's own chips, and the deal lands as Amazon prepares to sell its Trainium chips more widely. Cheaper compute means cheaper training and faster answers, and that is exactly where Nvidia's rivals need to close the gap. Via T L D R A I.
And third, Europe's fintech funding is splitting in two. Sifted data shows Series B and C fintech deals fell forty-eight per cent between twenty twenty-five and this year, while the average round size rose by almost half: fewer companies, bigger cheques. Spend management firm Payhawk raised two hundred and eighty million dollars despite the downturn, and London's Model M L, which builds A I for financial services, raised a two hundred and fifty million dollar Series B led by General Atlantic and Q E D. With Revolut not expected to list until twenty twenty-eight, early stage is where the energy is, and deals for A I-native fintechs jumped nearly three hundred per cent in the first half. Via Sifted.
Now, over to policy and geopolitics.
Section four, policy and geopolitics.
First, Washington goes after remote access to A I chips. C S I S analysts unpack the Commerce Department's new rule, which formally replaces the Biden-era A I diffusion framework. Instead of global country-by-country quotas, it requires licences for a group of high-risk countries, plus a worldwide licence whenever companies headquartered in China or other arms-embargoed countries rent serious computing power from data centres anywhere. The catch is that exporters must now gather enough information from foreign data centres to prove they have checked who their customers are, without being told what enough means. Expect over-compliance, and nervousness among cloud and data centre operators across Asia. Via C S I S.
Second, the real question behind the Nvidia saga: who sets American tech policy? International Intrigue argues the episode is a proxy fight between Washington's growth-at-all-costs faction and its national security hawks. On the same day Huang returned, the government finally blacklisted Megaspeed, the firm accused of channelling Nvidia computing power to China, and Senator Tom Cotton is now promising both an investigation and a tougher chip export bill. With Democrats taking control of Congress in January, anyone dealing with American export controls should expect more volatility, not less. Via International Intrigue.
And third, two quieter moves worth knowing. The United States Trade Representative has extended all one hundred and seventy-eight existing exclusions from tariffs on Chinese imports until the ninth of January, citing ongoing talks with Beijing. And the White House A I task force has recommended limiting regulatory liability for companies hit by A I-driven cyberattacks, with at least twelve months' grace for firms that report problems in good faith. Both are signs of a government trying to manage disruption rather than add to it. Via C S I S.
Now, over to community, events and marketing.
Section five, community, events and marketing.
One idea worth stealing: build communities of commitment. David Spinks argues that the most valuable groups are not the ones that answer questions or throw good parties, but small circles where you say your commitments out loud and the same people ask you about them next time. He cites research showing that simply announcing a goal can backfire, because being heard gives you a false sense of having arrived. What works is coming back, week after week, to people who remember what you said. If you run a founder or community programme, design for that return visit, not the launch moment. Via David Spinks.
And a second, from events: when a neighbourhood becomes your venue, you inherit every job a convention centre usually does. The first B twenty U S A summit spread its programme across fourteen venues on Washington's waterfront, loaded in on a single day, and used so much L E D screen that it exhausted the local supply, leaving a sixty-foot ticker dark during the opening concert. Power, wifi, loading docks and security queues all became the organiser's problem. Skift's second tip is timely: with Thanksgiving travel projected to fall for the first time since two thousand and eight, mainly because of cost, watch registration pace early and be ready with value-adds for self-funded attendees. Via Skift.
Now, over to one interesting thing.
Section six, one interesting thing.
Why do people love the streets of Osaka and Taipei, even though the buildings are mostly ordinary? Works in Progress revisits the Austrian architect Camillo Sitte, whose eighteen eighty-nine book argued that beloved places are small, enclosed outdoor rooms, not grand symmetrical plazas. His rules of thumb still hold: a square should be no wider than twice the height of its main building, statues belong at the edges rather than the centre, and great buildings look grander when they are tangled up with everyday housing rather than standing alone. It is a useful lens for anyone designing a space where people gather, from a city block to an event venue. Via Works in Progress.
That's all for today. Thanks for listening to Byte-sized, and have a good Wednesday.

item.title: Byte-sized — Tuesday, 24 November
item.description:
Good morning, and welcome to Byte-sized for Tuesday the twenty-fourth of November. Six sections today, starting as always in Japan and the Asia Pacific.
Section one, Japan and Asia Pacific.
First, a Korean chipmaker now sits at the top of Kioxia's shareholder register. S K Hynix has become the largest shareholder in Kioxia, Japan's flash memory champion, with an indirect stake of about fourteen per cent. It got there by converting bonds held through an investment vehicle into shares and buying a small extra block from Bain Capital, which takes it past Toshiba, now on roughly ten and a half per cent. Coming straight after yesterday's warnings about a global memory squeeze, this matters: one of Japan's few strategic semiconductor assets is increasingly tied to a Korean rival, and Tokyo will be watching how much say S K Hynix expects to have. Via T L D R Hardware.
Second, Taiwan's chip giant pulls back from China. T S M C has reportedly told Chinese chip designers to stop placing orders at sixteen nanometres and below unless they hold an American licence, after new United States rules presumed those chips to be controlled. That pushes Chinese customers back onto older twenty-eight and forty nanometre processes. In the same newsletter, the Chinese humanoid robotics startup Simplexity raised one hundred million dollars at a one point six billion dollar valuation, in a round led by Ant Group with Alibaba and Tencent also on board, a reminder that China's robotics push is being funded at home whatever happens to its chip supply. Via T L D R Hardware.
And third, India makes it easier to visit. India has cut its visa categories from thirteen to nine, halved the sub-categories, and reduced the information applicants must supply by as much as seventy per cent. A new visitor visa lets people combine leisure, business, wellness and medical trips, with up to ten years' validity for repeat visitors. Skift's point is that paperwork is only the start: arrivals fell nearly ten per cent last year to nine point two million, and India still needs hotel rooms, marketing and flights. Meanwhile Vietnam is adding routes from Delhi, Bengaluru and Ahmedabad to catch India's outbound boom, with Indian arrivals there up a third this year. Via Skift.
Now, over to A I and tech.
Section two, A I and tech.
First, the Riemann hypothesis may have fallen. Levent Alpöge, a mathematician at Anthropic, says that working with Claude over about six weeks he has proved the Riemann hypothesis, the one hundred and sixty-seven year old question about the pattern of prime numbers that carries a one million dollar Millennium Prize. The proof was released as a library of some seventeen million lines of machine-checkable code, and the communities behind the Lean verification language say they have full confidence it is correct. The catch is that no human yet fully understands it, and one group of mathematicians has dismissed it as publicity for A I labs. Whatever the arguments, a problem experts expected to take decades of new theory has been checked by machine in weeks. Via The Rundown A I and T L D R A I.
Second, Anthropic's listing is done, and the numbers are enormous. Anthropic closed its initial public offering at eighty-three dollars a share, raising about ninety-three and a half billion dollars, and listed on Nasdaq. Alongside it, A M D, Broadcom, Google, Micron, Microsoft, Nvidia and T S M C put in another twenty-six billion through a private placement, bringing the total to around one hundred and nineteen and a half billion. Sifted reports a first-day valuation of about one point seven six trillion dollars, followed by a bruising tech sell-off on Friday and expectations of continued volatility. Investors say the real test is whether the market rewards growth or demands profitability, and how it judges Anthropic's huge compute commitments. Via Sifted and T L D R Fintech.
Third, Jensen Huang is back at Nvidia. Only days after his departure, the board has reinstated him as chief executive, and Nvidia added roughly a trillion dollars of market value as a result. The board's statement said it had taken input from senior levels of the United States government and was confident his return posed no national security risk. That follows reports that American intelligence had tracked contacts between a Singapore chip-cloud executive and China's Ministry of State Security. Byrne Hobart's reading is blunt: Nvidia has effectively become a defence contractor, and its board now partly ratifies decisions made in Washington. Via The Diff and T L D R Hardware.
And fourth, the fine print on A I agents and your bank account. Citi's updated customer agreement treats anything an A I agent does with account access as authorised by the customer, even when the agent goes beyond its instructions, and that extends to credentials the agent leaks. Citi's own tools are exempt. At the same time, Stripe has opened a preview that lets agents pay suppliers and move funds under approval rules, for example allowing small transfers automatically and sending larger ones to a human. The lesson for anyone deploying agents: liability is being settled in terms and conditions right now, mostly in the provider's favour. Via T L D R Fintech.
Now, over to startups and venture.
Section three, startups and venture.
First, Europe's angels hit the jackpot. Sifted reports that dozens of European angel investors hold Anthropic shares, led by the Skype cofounder Jaan Tallinn, who led the company's Series A in twenty twenty-one, a bet now estimated to be worth tens of billions. One British angel who put in two hundred and fifty thousand dollars in twenty twenty-four is looking at roughly a sixteen-fold return. Meanwhile Atomico's annual State of European Tech report shows European investment in compute and intelligence more than doubling to twenty billion dollars, though that is still a fourteenth of the American figure, and early-stage startups are finding it harder to raise. Via Sifted.
Second, the fintech scoreboard. Ramp is in early talks to raise at least a billion dollars at a valuation above seventy billion, its third round in a year. In the other direction, Intuit has sold Mailchimp to Bending Spoons for three point six eight billion dollars, less than a third of the twelve billion it paid in twenty twenty-one, and Rogo, founded by former junior bankers to automate finance grunt work, is raising three hundred and fifty million dollars at a three point seven five billion valuation. Momentum is rewarded, and yesterday's growth darlings are being sold for parts. Via T L D R Fintech.
And third, a warning for founders setting a price. The V C Corner argues that most founders anchor their valuation on recently funded competitors, which is a mistake: those numbers are receipts from companies that already found willing investors, not a guide to what you will get. With roughly half of venture-backed companies now sitting below their last valuation, the advice is to price your own round from your stage, sector and growth, and remember that a higher number is not always better if it sets you up for a down round. Via The V C Corner.
Now, over to policy and geopolitics.
Section four, policy and geopolitics.
First, the climate summit collapses. COP thirty-one in Turkey ended on Sunday with no overarching deal, the first time in many years, after becoming the longest summit on record. The sticking points were familiar: oil producers watering down language on fossil fuels and pushing carbon capture, rich countries pledging just fifty million dollars in new adaptation money, and a loss and damage fund holding far less than poorer countries are asking for. Underneath it all is the consensus rule, which lets any bloc block a deal. Only one G7 leader turned up, and none of the three biggest emitters. Via International Intrigue.
Second, a tax on building data centres abroad. President Trump has promised what he called a tremendous tax on American companies that build data centres overseas, naming a proposed Google facility in Finland. The stated concern is that Chinese firms rent restricted chips from data centres in countries that can legally import them. For Japanese and other allied governments courting American cloud investment, this is a new risk to price in. Via T L D R Hardware.
And third, the race for the United Nations' top job is stuck. The Security Council's ninth straw poll ended in another stalemate, with all eight candidates facing at least two possible vetoes from the permanent members. António Guterres's term ends on the thirty-first of December, and International Intrigue warns the United Nations could start the new year without a Secretary-General. Via International Intrigue.
Now, over to community, events and marketing.
Section five, community, events and marketing.
One idea worth stealing: write the proposal in the buyer's own words. The Rundown's head of sales records discovery calls, has A I pull out exactly what the buyer asked for, and drafts the proposal from that rather than from a rate card. He also adds a smaller yes option, so too expensive becomes let's test it. The result is a proposal sent within about ten minutes, while the buyer still cares. The same trick works for sponsorship decks and event partnerships. Via The Rundown A I.
And a second, shorter one: when growth stalls, check the whole system before reaching for a new tactic. Chenell Basilio of Growth in Reverse says most newsletter creators chase the next platform hack when the problem is one of five connected levers they have ignored. It applies just as well to communities and event series: audit the system first. Via Growth in Reverse.
Now, one last thing.
Section six, one interesting thing. How can biotech hedge funds possibly know more than the scientists running the trials? Works in Progress argues that a surprising number of clinical trial results are predictable to anyone willing to look, because some very expensive trials repeat designs that have failed many times before. One published model, using only basic features of the drug target and the trial design, predicted Phase Two outcomes ahead of time with seventy-nine per cent accuracy. The edge, it turns out, is not secret knowledge, just the discipline to read the base rates everyone else ignores.
That's Byte-sized for today. Thanks for listening, and see you tomorrow.

item.title: Byte-sized — Monday, 23 November
item.description:
Good morning, and welcome to Byte-sized for Monday the twenty-third of November. Six sections today, starting as always in Japan and the Asia Pacific.
Section one, Japan and Asia Pacific.
First, Nippon Steel gets to work on an American icon. After its long and politically fraught takeover of U S Steel, the Japanese steelmaker is now trying to bring the American company's ageing plants back to life, starting with its oldest mill outside Pittsburgh. This is the part of the deal that never made headlines during the fight in Washington: the slow, expensive work of modernising old American capacity with Japanese capital and methods. If it works, it becomes the template people in Tokyo point to when they say Japanese investment is the friendly way to reshore American industry. Via Why Is This Interesting.
Second, a sobering number on Taiwan. A new C S I S study by Seth Jones and Daniel Byman, with Eric Heginbotham, asks whether China's People's Liberation Army is really ready for a fight. Their headline figure: if an invasion of Taiwan were launched this year, China's entire amphibious fleet would come to fewer than one hundred ships, backed by about eighty landing craft. That fleet is the centre of gravity of any invasion, and it is a small set of targets set against the large stocks of missiles and drones held by Taiwan and the United States. For Japan, whose southern islands sit right next to any such operation, the study is a useful corrective to the idea that an invasion is simply a matter of when Beijing decides. Via C S I S.
Now, over to A I and tech.
Section two, A I and tech.
First, travel wants its own A I. The Phocuswright Conference in Fort Lauderdale drew more than a thousand travel executives last week, and the most-read idea was that the general models from the big labs simply have not seen enough travel data to plan and book trips well. That is the opening Booking Holdings is going for: it has formally launched its combined business-to-business arm, the Booking Partner Division, led by Omri Morgenshtern, who also runs the Singapore-born Agoda, and is pitching it as the travel brain that the large language models plug into. Elsewhere, Sabre is bringing conversational booking to Grok, Kayak added twenty-eight A I features, and Airbnb is aiming to launch its own agent in the first half of twenty twenty-seven. The pattern: the companies that own the inventory want to be the layer agents depend on, rather than the layer agents route around. Via PhocusWire.
Second, stop describing your style to A I, and show it instead. Every's head of evaluations, Mike Taylor, has been trying to get A I to write like him since twenty twenty. What finally worked was not a description of his voice but a test. He took a couple of dozen of his own published pieces, stripped each one down to a plain brief, had a model draft from each brief, and then asked a separate A I judge which of two drafts sounded more like the original, swapping the order to cancel out bias. He kept only the changes to his writing instructions that raised the score. The striking result is that a writing skill tuned to one particular model can beat a stronger model running generic instructions. He now goes from an opinion to a finished piece in about an hour instead of a day. Via Every.
Third, where enterprise A I money is actually going. Menlo Ventures reports that health care A I spending grew two and a half times this year to three point seven billion dollars, more than double legal, the next biggest vertical. Pharmaceutical A I spending rose twenty-three-fold to seven hundred million dollars, and Microsoft and Epic captured more than two thirds of new spending on ambient scribes, the tools that write up a doctor's notes while they talk to a patient. Separately, the chief executive of Baseten argues that inference, the cost of actually running models, could become a two trillion dollar market by twenty thirty, though the newsletter fairly notes that his revenue forecasts have missed every year since twenty twenty-three. Via The V C Corner.
And fourth, A I and the twenty twenty-six election: less disinformation than feared, but one new weakness. Researchers at Caucus A I found that fake content mostly failed to move voters, who were already dug in. The more interesting finding was that the models themselves could be fooled: when researchers set up fake campaign websites for real politicians, and for races that did not exist, chatbots cited them as sources. The Diff's Byrne Hobart reads that as a good outcome, because now that the trick is known, the models will work harder to find official sources. Via The Diff.
Now, over to startups and venture.
Section three, startups and venture.
First, how much of venture capital is now Nvidia. PitchBook counts two hundred and nineteen and a half billion dollars of venture deals involving Nvidia so far this year, more than a quarter of all global venture value. Seven frontier labs account for about eighty per cent of that money, despite being barely six per cent of the deals. That concentration is why Jensen Huang's departure as chief executive on the twelfth of November matters to founders who never sold a chip: many of those mega-rounds were built on personal relationships, and the chief financial officer, Colette Kress, is serving as interim chief executive while the search goes on. Via The V C Corner.
Second, Europe is having its second-best year ever. European tech investment is projected to reach eighty-one billion dollars in twenty twenty-six, up sixty-two per cent from last year and second only to the ninety-four billion of twenty twenty-one. Thirteen rounds of a billion dollars or more have raised twenty-two billion between them, a new European record and more than a third of the total. Among the week's big deals: Genesis A I raised five hundred million dollars for general-purpose robotics, Science Corporation raised four hundred million for brain-computer interfaces and restoring vision, and Model M L raised two hundred and fifty million for A I agents in financial services. Via The V C Corner.
And third, a case for going early. A seed fund ran Howard Marks's five questions about investing in an unpredictable A I market and concluded that early-stage investing fits best. Its numbers: a roughly ninety-seven per cent chance that a portfolio of fifty companies returns its capital, and A I businesses under one hundred million dollars of revenue valued at a median of four point eight times revenue, against roughly twenty-seven times for Anthropic's private rounds. It is a self-interested argument, but the valuation gap between the frontier and everyone else is real. Via The V C Corner.
Now, over to policy and geopolitics.
Section four, policy and geopolitics.
First, the memory chip squeeze. C S I S warns that the United States faces an increasingly sharp shortage of memory chips, because the few suppliers are prioritising high bandwidth memory for the hyperscalers building A I data centres, which now take up to seventy per cent of available capacity. That leaves ordinary electronics makers short and tempts them towards Chinese memory, which C S I S argues brings security risks of its own. For anyone in procurement, memory is the quiet bottleneck behind next year's hardware prices. Via C S I S.
Second, Africa is shopping for new partners. American direct investment in Africa has fallen from a peak of sixty-nine billion dollars in twenty fourteen to under thirty-eight billion last year, while Chinese lending collapsed from nearly twenty-nine billion in twenty sixteen to about two billion in twenty twenty-four. C S I S says that gap is being filled by middle powers, especially in the Gulf. It is the same story Japan is playing out in Southeast Asia: when the great powers pull back, the middle powers with money and patience move in. Via C S I S.
And third, will A I growth reach the developing world? A new National Bureau of Economic Research paper models a world where A I services are traded globally, and warns that poorer countries could be left behind, lacking the complementary skills to use A I and being priced out by lower productivity. Tyler Cowen pushes back: A I already improves rainfall prediction and crop management, so it will not only help rich-country lawyers, and law in poorer countries is so bound up with politics that local lawyers are protected anyway. He expects the gap between rich and poor countries may widen, but poor countries still end up better off than without A I. Via Marginal Revolution.
Now, over to community, events and marketing.
Section five, community, events and marketing.
One idea worth stealing: give every talk a take-home tool. Every has turned each filmed talk from its first conference, Thesis twenty twenty-seven, into a skill file that attendees can install in their A I agent and use to apply the speaker's method to their own work. One, from a session on dividing work between people and agents, uses what they call a compound sandwich: you decide what to build at the start and judge the result at the end, and agents do the work in between. There are twenty-three in all. For anyone running events, it is a neat answer to the old problem that conference talks are forgotten by Monday: package each talk as something people can use, not just rewatch. Via Every.
And one for community builders. Pam Warhurst co-founded Incredible Edible, which links more than one hundred and twenty groups across the United Kingdom and over seven hundred worldwide, in school gardens, orchards, hospital grounds and high streets. The lesson is in the Do Lectures' own summary: one local act, a global movement. Start with something visible that anyone can copy, and let the copying be the growth strategy. Via The Do Lectures.
Now, over to one interesting thing.
Section six, one interesting thing.
Daughters may help keep parents alive. Using Danish records, researchers compared parents of only children who had a stroke at the same age and differed only in whether their child was a son or a daughter. Five years later, parents of daughters were one and a half percentage points more likely to be alive, and daughters were more likely to move nearer, less likely to be married and had fewer children. The surprising part is that parents of daughters also used more professional rehabilitation, which suggests that family care does not replace formal care so much as help people actually use it. Via Marginal Revolution.
That's all for today. Thanks for listening to Byte-sized, and have a good week.

item.title: Byte-sized — Week in review, 22 November
item.description:
Good morning, and welcome to Byte-sized for the week of the sixteenth of November. This is the Sunday week in review: six sections, the stories that still matter now the week is over, starting as always in Japan and the Asia Pacific.
Section one, Japan and Asia Pacific.
Where the week landed: a marathon of summits from Manila to Shenzhen produced plenty of symbolism and very little that binds anyone, and the real story for Japan was its quiet, steady build-out of influence in Southeast Asia while Washington's attention drifted.
First, Japan is acting like Southeast Asia's middle power. The C S I S Southeast Asia Program put the pieces together on Friday. Vietnam's leader, To Lam, made the first visit to Tokyo by a Vietnamese Communist Party general secretary in eleven years and signed ten agreements with Prime Minister Takaichi, aiming for one hundred billion dollars in two-way trade by twenty thirty, plus help with small modular nuclear reactors. The Philippines received Japan's largest ever security assistance grant, for coastal radar and surveillance drones. Malaysia's Petronas got a six hundred million dollar credit line. And at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation meetings in Shenzhen, of all places, Thailand's prime minister backed linking the A SEAN power grid to Japan's Asia Zero Emission Community. The pattern is consistent: Southeast Asian governments want Chinese money, but they want a Japanese option too, and Tokyo is supplying it through energy, finance and security rather than headlines. Via C S I S and International Intrigue.
Second, the summits themselves, and what they mean for Tokyo. Over five days, President Trump attended the A SEAN summit in Manila, held his first in-person Quad meeting of this term with Japan, India and Australia, went to Shenzhen for the Asia-Pacific forum, and sat down with Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin together for the first time. The Quad got fifty-five minutes, a business forum for twenty twenty-seven and a thinly sketched maritime surveillance plan. The three-way summit produced a photo opportunity and a joint line that a nuclear war must never be fought. The South China Sea code of conduct is still unfinished after more than twenty years. The worry in Tokyo is less any single result than the framing: a world of great-power spheres leaves allies like Japan and South Korea wondering where they sit, and C S I S's Korea Chair spent the week asking whether a separate Trump and Kim Jong Un channel is back in play. Prime Minister Takaichi did at least use the East Asia Summit to question China's conduct at sea. The quiet winner worth reading closely is A SEAN's new Digital Economy Framework Agreement, the region's first legally binding deal of its kind. Via International Intrigue and C S I S.
Third, rare earths: still the pressure point. The week opened and closed with the same C S I S finding: a year after the Busan truce, American rare earth imports from China remain almost seventy-five per cent below their earlier level, and Beijing's selective controls hit America and Japan hardest. In between, Malaysia granted France an exemption from its ban on raw rare earth exports in return for local investment, and an American consortium beat Australian and Chinese rivals for Kenya's Mrima Hill deposit. The lesson for Japanese manufacturers is that critical minerals are now traded for factories and diplomatic favours, not simply bought, and that Japan's fifteen years of diversification since twenty ten were money well spent. Via C S I S and International Intrigue.
And fourth, close to home in Fukuoka. Sunday's mayoral election produced no winner: thirteen candidates, none reaching the legal threshold of a quarter of the vote, so the city must hold a completely fresh contest, not a run-off. Meanwhile Kyushu's food brands are being snapped up, with Skylark agreeing to buy the Hakata ramen name Shin-Shin for about twelve billion yen and another chain, Ikkousha, going to a Tokyo fund. A city that sells itself on stability now has a stretch of caretaker politics, and regional brands are being repackaged for export. Fukuoka Now's Kyushu Roundtable picks over the election on the fourth of December. Via Fukuoka Now.
Now, over to A I and tech.
Section two, A I and tech.
Where the week landed: every major lab shipped something, none of the launches settled the race, and the bigger shift was in how A I is bought, governed and paid for.
First, the model race got crowded and confusing. OpenAI released G P T six point two Astra and the cheaper Sol to rough reviews, with no real improvement in coding and OpenAI's own safety team putting Astra at its high threshold for self-improvement, a first for a public model. Google shipped Gemini four Neon, its fourth Gemini four release in under two months, which scores near the top of the independent rankings at roughly a quarter less than rivals, though its bigger sibling Carbon still struggles to stop once it starts. Microsoft released seven good-enough models at low prices, including a coding model that reaches about ninety-eight per cent of OpenAI's quality at about forty per cent of the cost. Anthropic's Fable five point two still sits at the top of the independent index. For anyone buying A I for a team, the takeaway is that cheap and good options are multiplying faster than the headline frontier, so benchmark on your own tasks, not on launch-day claims. Via The Rundown A I, T L D R A I and Every.
Second, Nvidia without Jensen Huang. The week started with a petition of more than a hundred and forty thousand signatures, Elon Musk's among them, demanding his return, and the Treasury Secretary calling for an outsider. Then Nvidia reported about one hundred and sixteen billion dollars of quarterly revenue, up a hundred and three per cent, guided to around a hundred and thirty billion while assuming nothing from China, and its board chair said Huang would not be reinstated. Huang himself admitted serious mistakes and testifies before Congress on the first of December. And still the shares fell: by Friday Nvidia had roughly halved from its October record. That gap between results and price is the story of section three. Via International Intrigue, The Rundown A I and The V C Corner.
Third, agents got wallets, and businesses had to choose a side. OpenAI's ChatGPT Wallet lets an agent buy things without ever seeing your card, with a face or fingerprint check on every purchase. Google's Gemini app can now call businesses and shop within a limit you set. Andreessen Horowitz says agent browsing traffic grew eightfold between August and October. But Amazon and United Airlines block shopping agents, because their margin lives in extras that agents skip, while Shopify welcomes them. SaaStr found that when one vendor raised prices by forty per cent, its own agents cut their calls by ninety. Whether you welcome agents, and how you price for them, now depends on exactly where your profit comes from. Via T L D R, Every and Sifted.
And fourth, the enterprise wants to own its A I, and the courts want a say. Satya Nadella told Every that a world run by one A I company will not happen, and Microsoft now lets large customers license and run its model weights in their own cloud. Palo Alto Networks is paying four and a half billion dollars for Applied Compute for the same reason. At the same time, California sued OpenAI over last summer's agent escape, claiming more than eighty incidents against twenty-seven made public, and OpenAI's cyber model helped find a serious flaw in Java while NATO's cyber agency signed up to use it. A I is now firmly on both sides of security, and on both sides of the courtroom. Via Every, T L D R I T, The Rundown A I and T L D R InfoSec.
Now, over to startups and venture.
Section three, startups and venture.
Where the week landed: the biggest stock market listing in history went well, and the market around it did not.
First, Anthropic goes public. It priced above range at eighty-three dollars a share, raising eighty-one point three billion dollars, plus a twenty-six billion dollar private placement at the same price, and valuing the company at about one and a half trillion dollars. It opened on the Nasdaq at one hundred and eleven dollars fifty and closed day one up seventeen per cent. Ninety-six per cent of its staff are now paper millionaires, and the co-founders have pledged eighty per cent of their shares to charity. The detail that matters most came on Friday: in the worst week for American shares since April last year, Anthropic still closed about six per cent above its offer price. Tyler Cowen, who discloses an advisory role with the company, made the contrarian point that a firm expecting superintelligence imminently would borrow rather than sell shares, so the listing signals sensible expectations. Via The Rundown A I, Sifted, Marginal Revolution and The V C Corner.
Second, the A I selloff. The V C Corner tallied the damage: the S and P five hundred is in a correction, more than eleven per cent off its October record, with roughly eight trillion dollars of value gone in forty-five days. Nvidia, A M D, Micron and Broadcom each fell twelve to fourteen per cent on Friday alone, and Taiwan's tech-heavy index lost eighteen per cent on the week. Five things hit at once: the big cloud companies are spending more than they earn and borrowing to fund data centres, Democrats won Congress, the Federal Reserve looks set to raise rates again in December, Nvidia lost its founder, and the giant listings soaked up investors' cash. Yet company earnings and A I revenue keep rising. The writer's read is that cheap financing for A I has ended, not demand for it, and that firms funding their build-out from their own cash will come out stronger. Via The V C Corner and International Intrigue.
Third, what it means for founders. A I took more than four out of every five venture dollars in America this year, and private valuations move last, so rounds priced early next year will be judged against this week's public prices. Early rounds are already at about half their twenty twenty-two levels, more venture-backed startups have shut down this year than in any year on record, and investors want software firms to reach a hundred million dollars in revenue within five years. Against that, the top of the market keeps raising: Isomorphic Labs took five billion dollars for A I drug discovery, Genesis A I raised five hundred million for a robot without a head, and in Europe Plural closed a one billion euro fund that only backs companies with a hundred-times upside. And Y Combinator's Fall batch, two hundred and thirty-five companies with a median team of two, pitches on the second of December. One Japan note: Tokyo's Sakana A I, an earlier Generalist Future fifty pick, is now valued at about two point seven billion dollars. Via The V C Corner, T L D R Founders, Sifted and The Generalist.
Now, over to policy and geopolitics.
Section four, policy and geopolitics.
Where the week landed: lots of diplomacy at the top, and real strain at the world's shipping chokepoints and in the compliance departments of banks and exporters.
First, the chokepoints. Geopolitical Monitor counts three hundred and seventeen merchant ships hit by drones in the Black Sea and the Sea of Azov between May and October, and concludes only a truce will reopen it. In Yemen, the internationally recognised government went in forty days from vowing to take the capital to retreating towards Aden, leaving Iran-aligned Houthi forces set to hold the Bab al-Mandeb, gateway to the Red Sea. Ukraine talks have restarted, with Europe naming its own negotiating team, and there is one hopeful signal: oil fell about a fifth in November as talks to end the Iran war gained ground. For anyone briefing on supply chains, two of the world's key sea routes are under strain at once. Via Geopolitical Monitor, International Intrigue and The V C Corner.
Second, compliance just got harder. The Inside Deutsche Bank leak, fifteen million documents, bigger than the Panama Papers, alleges Russian revenue concentrated in sanctioned clients, payments tied to North Korean fronts, and years without suspicious activity reports, and the bank's shares fell sharply. On export controls, C S I S says Washington has moved from engaging industry to simply enforcing, with rules changing through letters and website postings, while Southeast Asian countries including Singapore and Malaysia were added to the list of advanced chip diversion risks. Put together, expect banks and exporters to tighten due diligence quickly, and small and mid-sized Japanese suppliers to feel it first. Via International Intrigue, C S I S and Benedict Evans.
And third, a landmark ruling. The International Court of Justice found that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya, the first time it has ever held a state responsible for genocide. There is no appeal. For companies with Myanmar in their supply chains, the reputational risk has just risen sharply. Via International Intrigue and C S I S.
Now, over to community, events and marketing.
Section five, community, events and marketing.
Where the week landed: the best ideas this week were about building systems and rituals that keep going after the event ends.
The first idea worth stealing comes from C M X's Circuit Tour: ten events in nine cities, with many stops used to launch a local chapter whose leader co-hosted. The one-off event left behind a host and a next date, not just a thank-you email. If you run events across a region like Kyushu, design each stop to seed something that keeps meeting. Via C M X.
The second is from Ramp: treat your brand as infrastructure. Its designers handed routine decks and one-pagers to a Slack agent that builds from approved examples, with automatic checks before anything goes out, and every new hand-made piece becomes another example. Pair that with Every's tip of turning your corrections to an A I draft into simple yes or no checks, and a small community team can make its house style stick without becoming a bottleneck. Via T L D R Founders and Every.
And a third, for events in particular. A futurist told Skift Meetings that most conferences waste their stages, and suggested fewer keynotes and sponsors willing to drop their talking points. Skift added a practical warning after last weekend's American ground stop, which caused nearly twenty thousand cancellations and could cost the big airlines close to a billion dollars: most event contracts cover a cancelled event, not one where half your attendees arrive a day late. Check your force majeure clauses before the next one. And as gathering season begins, Priya Parker's advice holds: plan for the awkward small moments, not just the agenda. Via Skift and Priya Parker.
Now, over to one interesting thing.
Section six, one interesting thing.
The idea that stuck all week came from Dan Wang in Works in Progress. Most countries have one dominant city: Paris is seven times bigger than France's next largest, Seoul six times bigger than Korea's. America and China are different, with Beijing not even China's biggest city and Washington outside America's top five metro areas. Wang argues that this many-centred structure, with regions competing with the capital, is part of what lets both superpowers combine dynamism with a strong state. It is a thought worth holding onto as Fukuoka prepares to choose its mayor a second time.
That's it for the week. Thanks for listening to Byte-sized, enjoy your Sunday, and see you tomorrow.

item.title: Byte-sized — Saturday, 21 November
item.description:
Good morning, and welcome to Byte-sized for Saturday the twenty-first of November. Six sections today, starting as always in Japan and the Asia Pacific.
Section one, Japan and Asia Pacific.
First, Fukuoka has to vote again. Thirteen candidates stood in the city's mayoral election on the fifteenth of November, and not one of them won the share of the vote the law requires, so the whole contest has to be rerun. The parties are now rethinking who they back, the campaign poster boards have already come down ahead of the repeat vote, and the city is working out who runs things in the meantime. It is an unusual moment of uncertainty for a city that has sold itself to startups and foreign residents on stability and long-term planning, so the second round is worth watching. Via Fukuoka Now.
Second, Kyushu's ramen brands are being bought up. The restaurant group Skylark plans to buy Shin-Shin, one of Fukuoka's best-known Hakata ramen names, for about twelve billion yen, and to grow it to around three hundred restaurants in Japan and overseas within five years, while keeping its name, flavour and service. In the same week, another Hakata chain, Ikkousha, was sold to a Tokyo investment fund. The pattern is clear: big national players and funds see Kyushu's regional food brands as ready-made products for export. Via Fukuoka Now.
Third, a reminder of how exposed Japan still is on rare earths. One year after the Trump and Xi trade truce in Busan, the CSIS Critical Minerals Security Program finds that American rare earth imports are still nearly seventy-five per cent below where they were before China's restrictions. Beijing's selective export controls continue to hit America and Japan hardest, and CSIS argues for stronger enforcement before the next round of talks. Separately, the programme counts more than forty critical mineral agreements signed by the current American administration, though most are not legally binding. For Japanese manufacturers, the message is that the truce has not fixed the supply problem. Via CSIS.
And fourth, Asian markets have had a bruising week. Taiwan's tech-heavy stock index fell more than six per cent on Friday alone, taking its losses for the week to eighteen per cent, as worries about an A I bubble spread across Asian markets. Meanwhile, on the diplomatic side, Prime Minister Takaichi used the East Asia Summit to question China's behaviour in the South China Sea, even as the summit's final statement retreated to safer ground such as cracking down on the region's online scam centres. And closer to home, an N H K investigation counts at least thirty-four new Self-Defence Force units set up across Kyushu and Okinawa over the past decade. Via International Intrigue and Fukuoka Now.
Now, over to A I and tech.
Section two, A I and tech.
First, your A I agent now has a wallet. OpenAI has launched ChatGPT Wallet for a small group of American Pro subscribers: you add a card, ChatGPT's personal agent shops for you, and you approve each purchase with your face or fingerprint, without the agent or the shop ever seeing your card number. Every's team says it is comfortable letting agents handle purchases where the first reasonable option is fine, but still wants to press buy on anything that matters. Andreessen Horowitz is calling this the start of a business-to-agent economy, and says agent browsing traffic grew eightfold between August and October. If you sell anything online, it is time to ask how your products look to a machine, not just to a person. Via Every.
Second, enterprise A I is becoming about owning and governing your own models. Palo Alto Networks has agreed to buy Applied Compute for four and a half billion dollars in stock, gaining tools to train and run customised open-weight models across public and sovereign clouds. Microsoft has launched a managed service that lets companies set and enforce rules for how their A I agents behave, and Workday is creating an Irish company with a board of European Union citizens to run its sovereign cloud in Europe. Together with Microsoft's push this week to let large customers own their models, the direction is clear: big buyers want control, not just access. Via T L D R I T.
Third, teams of agents are starting to beat solo ones. In a Replit benchmark, a swarm of thirty-two A I agents sped up a data-processing workload almost nineteen times in two hours, against under four times for a single agent, though it used more computing power and worked best on tasks that could be split up cleanly. And Google says its open-source code review system for the Linux kernel, called Sashiko, now carries out about twelve hundred reviews a day, and is linked to a thirty-five per cent drop in follow-up bug fixes. Via T L D R A I and T L D R I T.
And fourth, what the room said at DealBook. The Rundown's Rowan Cheung reports that when the European Central Bank's Christine Lagarde was asked if A I is a bubble, the audience laughed nervously. Sam Altman argued hard that humans must stay in control, saying he does not want to end up as A I's pet Labrador, while Greg Brockman said the biggest difference between the labs will be who owns the computing power. Via The Rundown A I.
Now, over to startups and venture.
Section three, startups and venture.
First, Anthropic's first day as a public company. After pricing its shares at eighty-three dollars, Anthropic opened on the Nasdaq at one hundred and eleven dollars fifty, briefly valuing it close to two trillion dollars, and closed the day up seventeen per cent. Ninety-six per cent of its more than five thousand staff are now paper millionaires, and the co-founders have pledged eighty per cent of their shares to charity. At Slush in Helsinki, Menlo Ventures partner Deedy Das told Sifted the valuation was probably too low and called the listing a win for everyone building on these models, though Taiwan's market slide shows not every investor is so relaxed. Via The Rundown A I and Sifted.
Second, Plural raises one billion euros and sets a very high bar. The founder-led European fund has closed its third fund, four times the size of its first, just days after Sequoia shut its London office. Partner Khaled Helioui told The VC Corner that if Plural cannot see a hundred-times return, it does not invest, and it will pass on startups with great momentum if their best case is only thirty or forty billion dollars. Even with a billion euros, each partner signs just two or three new companies a year, with the focus on energy, A I infrastructure, defence and health. Via The VC Corner.
Third, the revenue behind the boom. Lovable, the A I app builder, has just turned two with more than six hundred million dollars in annual recurring revenue, and its playbook is less a growth hack than riding a fast-moving category, shipping big updates almost every week and asking every new hire to automate their own repetitive work. Stripe has also launched a weekly A I index tracking payments to around twenty thousand A I businesses: total A I revenue is up one hundred and three per cent on a year ago, but the typical company is growing much more slowly than the leaders. Via T L D R Founders.
Now, over to policy and geopolitics.
Section four, policy and geopolitics.
First, India at the halfway mark. Richard Rossow, who chairs India studies at CSIS, says the third Modi government has done well on trade, with tariff-focused agreements and fewer non-tariff barriers, and the feared crisis never came: growth hit seven point eight per cent in the first quarter, and foreign direct investment reached seventy billion dollars over the past year. But it has made just one foreign investment reform this term, compared with thirty-seven in its first, and the real bottlenecks of power, water, labour and land sit with the states. For Japanese companies weighing India as a China alternative, state-level policy is the thing to watch. Via CSIS.
Second, the summit season scorecard. International Intrigue's verdict on a marathon week from Manila to Shenzhen: the Quad held its first in-person leaders' meeting of the Trump era with modest results, the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum avoided every flashpoint, and the Trump, Xi and Putin meeting produced mainly a photo opportunity and a joint statement that a nuclear war must never be fought. Putin may now attend Trump's Group of Twenty summit next month. The takeaway for anyone briefing government or enterprise audiences: small clubs, plenty of symbolism, not much binding substance. Via International Intrigue.
And third, the race for minerals moves to Africa. An American consortium has beaten Australian and Chinese rivals for the rights to develop Kenya's Mrima Hill rare earth deposit, believed to hold around sixty billion dollars in critical minerals, though the Australian-led bidder is challenging the decision. It fits the pattern CSIS describes, of Washington taking a page from China's playbook by joining up foreign policy and industrial strategy. Via International Intrigue and CSIS.
Now, over to community, events and marketing.
Section five, community, events and marketing.
One idea worth stealing, from Priya Parker, ahead of the holiday gathering season. She tells the story of a self-confessed people-pleaser who, when an elderly neighbour got her son's name wrong at a family party, simply smiled and agreed. Parker's point is that gatherings are where groups quietly negotiate who we are, and her advice is to prepare for those small moments: practise staying calm rather than reacting, take twenty seconds to settle your body before you walk in, and sometimes talk less so the loudest person does not set the tone. For anyone hosting a community, the same applies: plan for the awkward micro-moments, not just the agenda. Via Priya Parker.
And a second, on getting your team to post. A piece in T L D R Founders argues that employee-led content can be a remarkably strong distribution channel, but that it dies quickly when companies hand out copy-and-paste captions, set posting quotas, or only push company news. People can smell a mandate. The takeaway: give your team permission and ideas, not scripts. Via T L D R Founders.
Now, over to one interesting thing.
Section six, one interesting thing.
How good are A I-written research papers? Tyler Cowen highlights work reported by The Economist: when one thousand economics papers produced by an automated A I research system were checked, none was error-free, and eight hundred and forty-two had at least one serious mistake. When a hundred human papers from the field's top journals were checked the same way, about one in ten had a grave error. But in a separate test where A I tried to reproduce forty-eight social science papers from their raw data, the better the model, the more the discrepancies turned out to be the humans' fault. Via Marginal Revolution.
That's it for today. Thanks for listening to Byte-sized, enjoy your Saturday, and see you tomorrow.

item.title: Byte-sized — Friday, 20 November
item.description:
Good morning, and welcome to Byte-sized for Friday the twentieth of November. Six sections today, starting as always in Japan and the Asia Pacific.
Section one, Japan and Asia Pacific.
First, Japan steps up as Southeast Asia's middle power. The CSIS Southeast Asia Program says the past fortnight showed how far Tokyo's role in the region has grown. Vietnam's leader, To Lam, made the first visit to Tokyo by a Vietnamese Communist Party general secretary in eleven years, and he and Prime Minister Takaichi signed ten agreements on trade, defence and energy, with a goal of one hundred billion dollars in two-way trade by twenty thirty. Japan also promised to help Vietnam bring in small modular nuclear reactors as early as twenty forty. On top of that, Japan gave the Philippines its largest ever security assistance grant, about twenty-seven million dollars for coastal radar and surveillance drones. Via CSIS.
Second, what came out of the ASEAN summit in Manila. President Trump arrived on the final day and joined the leaders of Japan, Australia and India for the first in-person Quad leaders' meeting of his second term. The Quad announced a business leaders' forum for twenty twenty-seven and a new maritime surveillance effort, though CSIS says details are thin. The big disappointment was the South China Sea code of conduct with China, which still is not finished after more than twenty years of talks; Manila put progress at somewhere between seventy-seven and ninety per cent, which tells you how far apart people still are on the basics. The quieter win was ASEAN's new Digital Economy Framework Agreement, the region's first legally binding deal of its kind, which aims to double the bloc's digital economy to two trillion dollars by twenty thirty. For Japanese firms selling into Southeast Asia, that digital agreement is the one to read. Via CSIS.
Third, Thailand makes a pitch for Japan's clean-energy network, from inside China. At the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation meetings in Shenzhen, Thailand's prime minister, Anutin, first charmed Chinese media in fluent Cantonese, then used his speech to back linking the ASEAN power grid to Japan's regional clean-energy initiative, the Asia Zero Emission Community. International Intrigue calls it a serious hedge: Southeast Asian governments want Chinese investment, but they also want options so they do not become dependent on Beijing. It also fits the CSIS picture of Tokyo using energy and climate finance, including a six hundred million dollar credit line for the Malaysian energy company Petronas, as a quiet form of influence. Via International Intrigue and CSIS.
And fourth, video games as Japanese soft power and supply chain story. With Grand Theft Auto Six finally out after a thirteen-year wait, International Intrigue looked at the geopolitics of gaming. Japan still takes about nine per cent of global consumer spending on games, behind only America and China, and Sony and Nintendo remain giants, though China's Tencent is now the largest company by market share. American tariffs pushed Sony and Nintendo into one of the fastest manufacturing moves in consumer tech, cutting China's share of consoles bound for America from eighty-six per cent to five per cent and making Vietnam number one. Japan scrapped its troubled Cool Japan investment fund this year, but it still aims to quadruple its content exports by twenty thirty-three. Via International Intrigue.
Now, over to A I and tech.
Section two, A I and tech.
First, Google's fast new model. Google has released Gemini four Neon, a quicker sibling of its top model, Carbon, and its fourth Gemini four release in under two months. Despite its mid-tier label, Neon scores sixty-one on the independent Artificial Analysis index, ahead of Carbon and behind only Anthropic's Fable five point two and OpenAI's Astra. It costs three dollars per million words in and fifteen out, roughly a quarter cheaper than its closest rivals. The Rundown notes that a Google researcher hinted, the night before launch, that self-improving A I may be behind the sudden pace. A separate test flagged by T L D R found Carbon taking almost an hour on bug fixes that rivals finished in minutes, so speed of shipping is not the same as speed of working. Via The Rundown A I and T L D R A I.
Second, Microsoft's counter-argument: as many models as firms. At a roundtable after his Ignite keynote, Satya Nadella told Every that a world run by one A I company will not happen, because customers will demand more than one supplier. Microsoft now lets large customers license the weights of its own models, run them inside their own cloud accounts, train them on their own data and decide when to upgrade. Microsoft says AT and T's custom model beat a leading OpenAI model on telecoms network tasks at one-fiftieth of the cost. Nadella also says former team leads are becoming individual contributors who manage agents, with their own budgets for A I usage. For enterprise buyers in Japan, owning a tuned model rather than renting a general one is becoming a real option. Via Every.
Third, A I is starting to design the chips it runs on. OpenAI says design changes suggested by its models shrank key parts of its own Jalapeño A I chip by an estimated ten to thirteen per cent, and working with A M D, the same approach improved some of A M D's flagship graphics chip designs by up to fourteen per cent. In a separate update, OpenAI says its agents now complete nearly half of research tasks that would take a person two to four hours. And a T L D R item reports that Anthropic spent nearly ten billion dollars on computing in the third quarter, with its compute spending growing about four times a year. Via T L D R A I.
Now, over to startups and venture.
Section three, startups and venture.
First, the largest stock market listing in history. Anthropic priced its shares at eighty-three dollars overnight, above its target range, raising eighty-one point three billion dollars and valuing the five-year-old company at about one and a half trillion dollars, ahead of its Nasdaq debut on Thursday. That beats SpaceX's raise to become the biggest initial public offering ever, and demand was about seven times the shares on offer. The economist Tyler Cowen, who discloses that he sits on an Anthropic advisory board, offers a contrarian read: if a company truly expected superintelligence very soon, it would borrow rather than share the upside with public investors, so the listing hints at sensible, not radical, expectations. Sifted has been saying European founders hope a strong debut frees up capital for their own A I companies. Via International Intrigue and Marginal Revolution.
Second, The Generalist's Future fifty is back. The annual list of the most promising startups valued at two hundred million dollars or less, nominated by partner-level investors, shows three trends. More than two thirds of this year's picks were founded in twenty twenty-four or later; nearly half have twenty or fewer staff, up from about a quarter two years ago; and America's share keeps growing. Of the hundred earlier picks, six were acquired and two are now worth more than ten billion dollars. One name worth noting for this audience: Tokyo's Sakana A I, an earlier pick, is now valued at about two point seven billion dollars. Via The Generalist.
Third, the bar for raising money keeps rising. Carta's latest American data shows that most early-stage SAFE notes end up converting at their valuation cap, so founders should treat the cap as the real price. SaaStr suggests venture investors now want software firms to grow from one million to one hundred million dollars in annual revenue within five years, and ideally two or three. More venture-backed startups have shut down this year than in any year on record. In Europe, Sifted reports the expense-management company Payhawk raised two hundred and eighty million dollars despite a wider fintech slump. Via T L D R Founders and Sifted.
Now, over to policy and geopolitics.
Section four, policy and geopolitics.
First, a landmark genocide ruling. The International Court of Justice has found that Myanmar committed genocide against its Rohingya minority, the first time the court has ever found a state responsible for genocide. The case was brought by The Gambia and took seven years. There is no appeal, and Myanmar could now face enforcement at the United Nations Security Council, where a veto from China or Russia would be more costly after this verdict. It lands days after ASEAN chose to keep Myanmar's military-backed leaders barred from its summits. For companies with supply chains in Myanmar, the reputational risk has just gone up. Via International Intrigue and CSIS.
Second, the three-way summit begins. Xi Jinping personally greeted President Trump on the tarmac in Shenzhen before their meeting with Vladimir Putin, and Trump declared, "we are making history". International Intrigue still expects little substance: Ukraine is not Trump's to give, Taiwan is not Xi's to take, and Putin is in no position to dictate terms. The CSIS Korea Chair ran a live discussion straight after the meeting, which is worth catching for the North Korea angle we flagged yesterday. Via International Intrigue and CSIS.
And third, a warning for anyone planning international events in America. Overseas visits to the United States have fallen for seven straight months, with October down about seven per cent on a year earlier. Surveys suggest costs and exchange rates are keeping Asian travellers away, while visitors from Canada, Germany and Australia cite the political climate, and the industry body does not expect a full recovery until twenty thirty. Skift suggests organisers stop assuming international attendees will bounce back, and consider regional events or moving meetings outside America every few years. Via Skift.
Now, over to community, events and marketing.
Section five, community, events and marketing.
One idea worth stealing, from a futurist who lives on conference stages. Henry Coutinho-Mason, who has advised many large companies, told Skift Meetings that most events waste their stages. His fix is fewer keynote speeches, and sponsors who are willing to drop their prepared talking points and actually engage. Skift adds a practical note from last week's nationwide flight ground stop in America: most event contracts cover a cancelled event, not one where half the attendees arrive a day late, so check your force majeure clauses for attendance drops. For your next event, try swapping one keynote for an unscripted sponsor conversation and see what the room does with it. Via Skift.
And a second idea, from McDonald's: the chef's table at the counter. McDonald's hired a Top Chef winner to host a one-day, reservation-only tasting called Inside the Golden Arches at a New York restaurant counter, where diners heard how a Quarter Pounder, an Egg McMuffin and the fries are actually made. Scan Club says it works because it pokes fun at fine dining while giving people real insider knowledge, which is exactly the kind of brand lore people want to share. The takeaway for community builders: a small, invitation-only, behind-the-scenes session about how your everyday thing is made can feel more special than a big launch. Via Scan Club.
Now, over to one interesting thing.
Section six, one interesting thing.
Colin Nagy at Why Is This Interesting shared a list of Tokyo cocktail bars that one hotel bar hands to curious guests, and one entry stands out. Rondo, in Kagurazaka, has just six seats and is devoted to traditional Japanese bartending; it is named after the musical form in which a theme keeps returning with variations, which suits a place built around repeat visits. It is a neat reminder that in Japan, the smallest venues often have the clearest idea of what they are for. Via Why Is This Interesting.
That's it for today. Thanks for listening to Byte-sized, have a lovely weekend, and see you tomorrow.

item.title: Byte-sized — Thursday, 19 November
item.description:
Good morning, and welcome to Byte-sized for Thursday the nineteenth of November. Six sections today, starting as always in Japan and the Asia Pacific.
Section one, Japan and Asia Pacific.
First, the three-way summit and the view from Tokyo. President Trump meets Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin together today, the first ever sit-down between the leaders of the three countries, with nuclear non-proliferation officially on the agenda. Xi used his warm-up talks with his "old friend" Putin to say Moscow and Beijing should lead the move towards a multipolar world. International Intrigue doubts any meaningful deal will come out of it, but argues that Xi and Putin still win simply by having an American president sit at the table and appear to accept their idea of great-power spheres of influence. The Council on Foreign Relations, flagged in the CSIS nuclear policy briefing, adds that a breakthrough on bringing China into arms control is unlikely. For Japan, that framing is the worry: any hint of carving up regions between big powers leaves allies like Tokyo and Seoul wondering where they sit. Via International Intrigue and CSIS.
Second, what it means for North Korea. The CSIS Korea Chair, Victor Cha, recorded a special episode of his podcast, The Impossible State, with the North Korea scholar Andrei Lankov and the Russia specialist Maria Snegovaya, on what the summit could mean for Pyongyang. The questions they focus on are what Putin hopes to gain, whether a separate Trump and Kim Jong Un meeting is back in play, and how the summit could reshape Russia's growing military partnership with North Korea. For Japan, any Trump and Kim channel that skips over abductions and short-range missiles is a familiar fear, so this is worth watching closely over the next few days. Via CSIS.
Third, Malaysia starts trading access to rare earths. On a state visit to Kuala Lumpur, President Macron raised France's ties with Malaysia to a strategic partnership and won an exemption from Malaysia's strict ban on exporting raw rare earths. Malaysia brought in the ban in twenty twenty-four to force more processing at home, but it created a bottleneck of stranded material, so the government is now easing the rules case by case for partners who invest locally. A French firm, Carester, announced a large local joint venture in July. Japan is one of the biggest players in Malaysian rare earths and has spent years building supply outside China, so the signal for Tokyo is clear: in Southeast Asia, access to critical minerals now comes in exchange for investment in local factories. Via International Intrigue.
And fourth, a political crisis in Mongolia. President Ukhnaa says he will resign over accusations, which he denies, that he took twenty-five million dollars in kickbacks from a huge railway project carrying coking coal into China. Mongolia has also had three prime ministers in nine months. That instability makes it harder for the landlocked country to keep up its "third neighbour" policy of balancing China and Russia with partners such as Japan, America and South Korea. Via International Intrigue.
Now, over to A I and tech.
Section two, A I and tech.
First, OpenAI's new models get rough reviews. OpenAI has released G P T six point two Astra, its top model, and G P T six point two Sol, a cheaper everyday model, in ChatGPT, its Codex coding tool and its developer platform. On the independent Artificial Analysis rankings, Astra now sits second, behind only Anthropic's Fable five point two, and Sol matches September's top model at roughly fifteen per cent of the cost per task. But there is no real improvement in coding, Sol actually slips backwards there, and some early testers were scathing, with one calling it the worst model OpenAI has released. OpenAI's own safety assessment also puts Astra at its "high" threshold for A I self-improvement, a first for a public release. The Rundown's read is that the timing is awkward, landing days before Anthropic goes public. Via The Rundown A I and T L D R A I.
Second, Nvidia keeps growing without its founder or China. Nvidia reported third-quarter revenue of about one hundred and sixteen billion dollars, with data-centre sales up a hundred and ten per cent, and guided to around a hundred and thirty billion dollars next quarter while assuming zero data-centre revenue from China. On the same call, the board chair said the company does not intend to bring back Jensen Huang, despite Huang's first public statement admitting "serious mistakes" and saying he would be honoured to return. Nvidia has set up an executive committee to oversee export-control compliance, and Huang testifies before Congress on the first of December. Via T L D R Hardware, The Rundown A I and International Intrigue.
Third, A I finds a hole in Java, and NATO buys in. A startup called Calif says OpenAI's cyber model helped it find a critical flaw in Java, the programming language running inside nine in ten of America's largest companies, which let it break into a login system used by NASA and CERN. Oracle shipped a fix on Tuesday. On the same day, OpenAI revealed that NATO's technology and cyber agency is using its security models to protect allied networks, and that Europe's cybersecurity agency has already used them to find four flaws in E U systems. After a month of attacks and outages, this is the clearest sign yet that A I is now on both sides of cyber defence. Via The Rundown A I and T L D R InfoSec.
And fourth, the cheaper end of the market gets crowded. Microsoft released seven new models built to be good enough at a low price, including a coding model in GitHub Copilot that reaches about ninety-eight per cent of OpenAI's coding quality at about forty per cent of the price. Google's Gemini app can now call businesses, book appointments and shop within a spending limit you set. For anyone buying A I for a team, the practical point is that "good and cheap" options are multiplying faster than the headline frontier models. Via T L D R A I.
Now, over to startups and venture.
Section three, startups and venture.
First, a five billion dollar round for A I drug discovery. Isomorphic Labs, the Alphabet-backed spin-out from DeepMind, has raised five billion dollars, co-led by Greenoaks and Sequoia, only six months after a two point one billion dollar round, at a reported valuation of around fifty billion dollars. The money pays for its drug-design engine, new foundational biology models, and its first programmes heading towards clinical trials, with partners including Eli Lilly, Novartis and Johnson and Johnson. Via Sifted and T L D R Hardware.
Second, robots and agents keep pulling in money. Genesis A I raised a five hundred million dollar Series A at a three and a half billion dollar valuation to build Eno, a wheeled robot with no head that skips the human form altogether. In London, Model M L, which builds personal A I agents for bankers, consultants and investors, raised two hundred and fifty million dollars led by General Atlantic and QED. And in Paris, Remanence raised a thirty million dollar seed round to turn the work traces of A I agents into specialised models whose weights the customer owns. Sifted also notes Europe is bracing for Anthropic's listing this week, with many hoping a strong debut frees up capital for the continent's own A I companies, and others fearing it could trigger a correction. Via Sifted and T L D R Hardware.
Third, the "SaaS-pocalypse" may be overstated. Software shares lost an estimated two trillion dollars earlier this year on fears that A I would replace business apps. But Stripe's new weekly index of non-A I software companies billing through its platform shows revenue up more than thirty per cent on a year ago. The caveats matter: most of those firms sell self-serve products paid by card, not the big enterprise names whose shares fell, and companies that shut down simply drop out of the index. Still, it is a useful corrective to the idea that ordinary software businesses have stopped growing. Via T L D R Founders.
Now, over to policy and geopolitics.
Section four, policy and geopolitics.
First, the biggest banking leak in history. A consortium of more than fifty newsrooms has published Inside Deutsche Bank, built on fifteen million leaked emails, chats and audits, which is larger than the Panama Papers.
