Before your next design conversation, ask what future this event is assuming, and then ask what happens if that future does not arrive. It is a cheap exercise that surfaces assumptions before they harden into decisions. Via Event Design Collective.
And a format worth borrowing from Fukuoka Now. Their Kyushu Roundtable on the thirtieth of October is built around a single question, what should Fukuoka prioritise after sixteen years under Mayor Takashima, with an architect and a long-time resident joining the publisher. It is free, in English, held in a small room with advance reservations only, and seats are limited. One question, three voices, a hard cap on seats: a simple recipe for a community evening people actually show up to. Via Fukuoka Now.
Now, one last thing.
Section six, one interesting thing.
In Why Is This Interesting's media diet, the former Google writer Claire Stapleton highlights a line from Gideon Lewis-Kraus's New Yorker essay on A I. Artificial intelligence has not cured cancer, but it has shown what happens when you concentrate an almost unimaginable amount of capital, engineering talent and political will on a single problem. That raises an awkward question: if society can mobilise like that for data centres, why does it insist that the same effort is impossible for housing, health or anything else it says it wants? Via Why Is This Interesting.
That is Byte-sized for today. Thanks for listening, and see you tomorrow.

item.title: Byte-sized — Week in review, 25 October
item.description:
Good morning, and welcome to Byte-sized, the week of the nineteenth of October. It is Sunday, so this is the week in review, in six sections, and we begin, as ever, in Japan and the Asia Pacific.
Section one, Japan and Asia Pacific.
Where the week landed: the region's story was about supply chains and who controls the critical pieces, from memory chips to rare earths, with Japan caught in the middle.
First, the chips. At the start of the week Tokyo Electron fell seven per cent in a single day, after news that China's memory maker CXMT had made progress on a new kind of high density memory and now holds around ten per cent of the global market. By midweek the picture was sharper: CXMT expects a nine month profit of nearly twenty billion dollars, against a small loss a year earlier, with revenue jumping from about four and a half billion to nearly thirty eight billion. The company credits shortages of memory driven by artificial intelligence. The caution is that memory booms end when new capacity floods the market, and its claim to have the latest generation in mass production is unverified. Even so, it explains why Japanese and Korean equipment makers have felt squeezed all week. Via International Intrigue and T L D R.
Second, rare earths. Japan may have only months, not years, before it runs out of yttrium, which goes into jet engines, semiconductors, electric vehicles and L E D lighting. China restricted exports last year, after Prime Minister Takaichi suggested Japan might respond in any war over Taiwan, and Tokyo is now lobbying Washington for help. If you sell into Japanese manufacturing, supply chain resilience is now a boardroom topic. Via International Intrigue.
Third, China's own numbers. Third quarter growth was four point five per cent, which keeps the five per cent target within reach, but retail sales are crawling at one per cent and property investment is down another twenty per cent this year. Growth is coming from state funded high technology manufacturing and record exports, which is to say Beijing is replacing weak confidence at home with subsidised demand abroad. Via International Intrigue.
Fourth, a quieter cluster of signals. Japan's bigger regional partners are also reshuffling: Vietnam signed a free trade agreement with the European Free Trade Association after fourteen years of talks, Accenture is reportedly exploring a sale of its Greater China consulting business for up to one and a half billion dollars, and the index provider MSCI is considering demoting Indonesia from emerging to standalone status, after which Jakarta's market fell eleven per cent in a day. The common thread is companies and investors hedging away from single points of exposure. Via International Intrigue and T L D R.
Fifth, closer to home for anyone in Kyushu. The Japan and United States Keen Sword exercise began on the nineteenth, running for eleven days across Kyushu and Okinawa. In Fukuoka, Mayor Takashima has said he will not name a successor ahead of November's election, after sixteen years in office. The plans for the former Kyushu University Hakozaki campus came into focus, with homes, research space, a major food destination and a proposed international school, and the Ramen Tech start-up week opened in Tenjin earlier this month. One small note for foreign residents: Nanzoin temple in Sasaguri now charges tourists five hundred yen, but residents of Japan enter free. Via Fukuoka Now.
Sixth, the artificial intelligence race, seen from Japan and China. Speeda's round-up for Japanese readers framed the debate over slowing down as a prisoner's dilemma, and made a sharper point about access: prices for models anyone can buy are falling fast, but the most capable systems are increasingly handed out by vetting rather than price. For Japanese firms the question is how to qualify for the top tier. Then on Friday, China's DeepSeek was reported to have raised about fifteen billion dollars, with Tencent and the battery maker C A T L among the backers, days after American agencies were told to remove its A I. Expect that to sharpen the debate in Tokyo and Seoul about which stack to build on. Via Speeda A I News, T L D R and The Rundown A I.
Seventh, two small Japan signals worth keeping. For the first time since the survey began in two thousand and eight, fewer than half of people in Japan, forty nine point eight per cent, now pay for a monthly newspaper subscription, a warning for anyone building subscription media. And Japan's space agency is set to launch its Martian Moons mission, aiming to bring a sample back from Phobos by twenty thirty one, a quiet showcase of Tokyo as a trusted deep space partner. Via International Intrigue.
Now, over to artificial intelligence and technology.
Section two, AI and tech.
Where the week landed: it was a week where artificial intelligence stopped being a product story and became an infrastructure and security story.
First, the biggest story of the week by far. Two critical flaws in P H P, the language behind roughly seventy per cent of websites, were found when researchers pointed powerful A I models at the code in August. Humans had dismissed the bugs as harmless memory quirks. Someone leaked details two days before the planned patch, and with A I help attackers built a working exploit in about six hours, a gap that used to be measured in weeks. Cloudflare reported thousands of attempts, then millions after the official announcement. America's National Security Agency told anyone who could not patch to take systems offline, and government sites in several European countries did just that. More than half of P H P servers run old versions that no longer get regular updates, so the clean up will be long. If you run a website, update this weekend. Via International Intrigue, The Rundown A I and T L D R.
Second, the agent economy arrived at the big suppliers. Anthropic launched Claude Duet, a personal agent that can act for you around the clock, with your sign off required before anything is deleted, paid or sent. Microsoft, meanwhile, described A I agents as akin to insider threats and launched Guardian Agents in Defender, while reportedly planning to pay Anthropic more than two billion dollars a year to use Claude in Copilot. And American banks say they are scrambling to detect and block unauthorised third party agents poking around customer accounts. The lesson of the week is separating the supply of intelligence from the authority over it. Via T L D R and The Rundown A I.
Third, what agents do to the companies building them. Anthropic reported that by August the hours worked by its employees' agents outnumbered human hours by six to one, junior staff fell from twenty seven per cent of technical hires to nine per cent, and engineers ship about five times as many code changes as six months ago. The Pragmatic Engineer added that Anthropic built its own source control system after Git struggled at thirty thousand pull requests a day, while a separate analysis of twenty seven companies asks whether higher A I spending has truly changed shipping speed. Via The Rundown A I and The Pragmatic Engineer.
Fourth, who pays for it all. OpenAI is reportedly closing in on a round at a valuation of about one point two five trillion dollars, led by investors from the United Arab Emirates. A Ramp index found that one per cent of firms account for eighty per cent of spending on the two leading labs, and OpenRouter reports that open weight models are about sixty per cent of tokens but only twenty six per cent of spending. Frontier capability is concentrating in a few hands while cheaper models carry the volume. Via T L D R.
Fifth, a few quick moves from the labs. OpenAI acquired Orchestra Bio, a platform that helps biopharma teams coordinate drug development, and is now also selling its models and Codex through Google Cloud, a sign that the old exclusive partnerships are loosening. Apple has confirmed an event on the twenty eighth of October in Los Angeles, where it is expected to show its first touch screen Macs. And Agility Robotics will use Nvidia's new computing modules as the exclusive onboard brain of the general sale version of its Digit humanoid, which tells you where physical A I is heading. Via T L D R.
Sixth, a note on the security side. Beyond P H P, the week brought a Capcom breach involving eleven point seven million accounts, malware in a popular A I developer library on the Python package index, and a leak of thousands of shared conversation links from Meta's new assistant, found through public domain name records. The pattern is the same: the tools are new, the mistakes are old. Via T L D R.
Now, over to start-ups and venture.
Section three, start-ups and venture.
Where the week landed: money is flowing, but toward a narrower set of winners, and increasingly toward the customers of the chip makers.
First, Sifted's analysis of Nvidia's European tour, which ended in Berlin: as in the United States, Nvidia tends to back the companies that buy its chips, so the largest sectors it has funded in Europe are compute buyers and A I cloud builders. Investors are divided on whether that is healthy. Via Sifted.
Second, the Nordic split. Stockholm start-ups have raised four and a half billion euros so far this year, more than double last year, led by Legora, which hit an eight point eight billion dollar valuation this week, and Lovable. Oslo has raised just two hundred and seventeen million euros, down from three hundred and forty million. As one Norwegian investor put it, the ultimate joy for a Norwegian start-up is to be sold really fast, and the missing piece is growth capital. Via Sifted.
Third, a reminder about fintech. Global fintech funding fell twenty one per cent, even as Ramp applied for a national trust bank charter and a code testing platform called Blacksmith reached a billion dollar valuation just two months after its previous round. Money is chasing infrastructure for the agent era. Via T L D R and Sifted.
Fourth, some European signals. Madrid's Seaya Nova raised six hundred million euros for a growth fund and is opening in London, and the median Italian early stage round this year is one point eight million euros, up from one million in twenty twenty four. Radical Ventures, the Canadian firm, has a new fund of more than a billion dollars and is betting on the wave of London labs founded by former DeepMind researchers. And a cautionary tale from The Generalist and others: Foursquare was acquired about a month ago, ending a seventeen year story as a zero dollar outcome for equity holders. Via Sifted and T L D R.
Fifth, the founder playbook. The V C Corner launched G R Angel, with fifty three companies backed, one point two billion dollars raised by those companies, one unicorn and a first exit, a company that went from one hundred thousand to seven million dollars in annual revenue in a year and sold to an A I lab before its Series A. And Indie Hackers profiled founders whose fifteen thousand dollar product bet, with a thirty thousand dollar loan hanging over them, now earns twelve thousand dollars a month selling templates. Via The V C Corner and Indie Hackers.
Now, over to policy and geopolitics.
Section four, policy and geopolitics.
Where the week landed: a week of pressure points where technology and security meet.
First, North Korea. A series of missile tests, a warning from Kim Yo Jong that border loudspeakers will be switched back on, and a C S I S discussion asking whether the launches are a prelude to a summit. Separately, C S I S estimates North Korea's overseas workers now number more than one hundred thousand across at least seventeen countries, earning the state hundreds of millions of dollars a year. Via C S I S and International Intrigue.
Second, the Pacific. The C S I S Australia Chair released an interactive map of who is partnering with whom on security across the Pacific islands, which is useful for any conversation about where influence is shifting, with New Zealand heading to the polls. Via C S I S.
Third, two items to watch today. Brazil votes in its presidential runoff, with polls showing the two candidates tied, and Ukraine says its Starlink connectivity is still throttled, even as the American president claims it is fixed. Via International Intrigue.
Fourth, trade and tech policy. The White House has opened new trade negotiations on wind turbines, about seventy eight per cent of which are made in China, after a national security investigation, which could mean more tariffs. C S I S's critical minerals programme and its Japan Chair continue to frame the same worry as the yttrium story: dependence on a single supplier is now a security issue, not just a cost issue. Via International Intrigue and C S I S.
Fifth, Europe. Chancellor Merz confirmed that Germany is the target of intense espionage after the arrest of a Ukrainian national suspected of passing military secrets to Russia, and Uncharted Territories asks why France has been in chaos, after weeks in which tens of thousands vandalised and burned schools, cars and shops. Founders in Paris are bracing for more uncertainty. Via International Intrigue, Uncharted Territories and Sifted.
Sixth, a health security note. Nigeria has reported its first confirmed Ebola case, as the outbreak centred on Congo becomes the second biggest in history. Via International Intrigue.
Now, over to community, events and marketing.
Section five, community, events and marketing.
Where the week landed: the best ideas this week were small, intimate and cheap to copy.
First, one idea worth stealing. Priya Parker posed what she calls a Magical Question at a family dinner spanning three children, several adults and her seventy eight year old father: what is something specific your mother or father did that made you feel really loved as a child? A question works when everyone is interested in answering it and in hearing everyone else's answer, and this one asked each person to be a child again, which equalised the table. Her father told two stories she had never heard. Use it at your next mixed generation gathering, or at the opening of a community event. Via Priya Parker.
Second, a format signal. Setlog, a Japanese and Korean app that asks you to record two seconds an hour and shares the stitched day only with chosen friends, has reached about ten million users in under a year, a sign that people are shrinking from public feeds into trusted circles. Scan Club also flagged a new app for closed communities. Marketing Brew, meanwhile, notes that brands are turning to analogue photography. Via Scan Club and Marketing Brew.
Third, an event idea worth borrowing. Fukuoka Now runs a free, English language Kyushu Roundtable at C I C Fukuoka, with a small panel and a clear theme. The next, on the thirtieth of October, is titled Fukuoka's Next Chapter and asks what the city should prioritise after sixteen years under one mayor. A single question, a local venue and a limited number of seats make for a format any community manager can copy. Via Fukuoka Now.
Now, one interesting thing to close.
Section six, one interesting thing.
A new paper traced how long wealth shocks persist in England, from seventeen hundred to today. The question is whether a windfall endures and even compounds across generations, or fades. The answer, in the title, is that it fades in less than three generations, which implies far less of today's wealth traces back to events before nineteen hundred than most of us assume. Via Marginal Revolution.
That's the week. Thanks for listening, and have a good Sunday.

item.title: Byte-sized — Saturday, 24 October
item.description:
Good morning, and welcome to Byte-sized for Saturday, the twenty fourth of October. Six sections today, and we begin, as ever, in Japan and the Asia Pacific.
Section one, Japan and Asia Pacific.
First, a Japanese read on the biggest argument in artificial intelligence. Speeda's A I News round-up for Japanese readers looks back at September, when the heads of Anthropic, OpenAI and xAI each voiced support for slowing down A I development, while the American president brushed the idea aside. The editors frame it as a prisoner's dilemma: any one company or country that slows alone loses ground, yet the shared resource of safety is quietly eroded if everyone keeps racing. Their sharper point is about access. Prices for models anyone can buy are falling fast, but the most capable systems are increasingly handed out by vetting rather than by price, to government bodies and approved organisations. For Japanese firms, the practical question becomes how to qualify for the top tier. Via Speeda A I News.
Second, China's DeepSeek has reportedly raised around fifteen billion dollars, one of the largest rounds in Chinese history, with Tencent and the battery maker C A T L among the backers. It comes just days after American federal agencies were ordered to remove its A I over security concerns, and as the company prepares for a possible public listing. Expect this to sharpen the debate in Tokyo and Seoul about which A I stack to build on. Via T L D R and The Rundown A I.
Third, two small signals from the region. North Korea's Kim Yo Jong has warned that the North will switch its border loudspeakers back on, in response to what she says are resumed broadcasts from the South. Seoul's earlier broadcasts would have followed a North Korean border mine that injured several of its soldiers last month. It is familiar territory, but it narrows the margin for error on one of the world's most heavily armed borders. And Malaysia has banned civil servants from using the Waze navigation app, citing national security concerns and the app's Israeli roots. Waze says it meets global data protection standards. Via International Intrigue.
Fourth, the C S I S Australia Chair has published an interactive tool mapping who is partnering with whom on security across the Pacific islands. If you are speaking with government people about the region, it is a handy way to see where influence is shifting. Via C S I S.
Now, over to A I and tech.
Section two, A I and tech.
First, OpenAI is closing in on a funding round of up to thirty billion dollars at a valuation of about one point two five trillion dollars, led by investors from the United Arab Emirates. It is being positioned as a bridge ahead of a possible public listing, with signatures targeted by the end of next week. Via T L D R.
Second, the P H P emergency, with new detail. International Intrigue's account is that researchers pointed powerful A I models at the code in August and found what humans had dismissed as harmless memory quirks, then quietly raced to patch. Someone leaked details two days before the planned release, and with A I help attackers built a working exploit in about six hours, a gap that used to be measured in weeks. Cloudflare has seen thousands of attempts, then millions after the official announcement. More than half of P H P servers run old versions that no longer get regular updates, so the clean-up will be long. The Rundown's advice for the weekend: update everything, and use a password manager and an authenticator app rather than text message codes. Via International Intrigue and The Rundown A I.
Third, a story that connects to it. America's biggest banks, including J P Morgan, Bank of America and Morgan Stanley, have found third-party A I agents logging into customer accounts with customers' own credentials, and sometimes doing things the customer never asked for. Morgan Stanley is blocking them outright, others are restricting them, and most are moving towards read-only access. One executive admitted they struggle to tell an authorised agent from a rogue one. In the same news cycle, 1Password launched a tool that lets agents log in to sites without ever seeing the password. The opportunity sits in identity and permissions for agents. Via The Rundown A I and T L D R.
Fourth, a reminder that the watchers need watching. METR and Redwood Research spent three weeks probing OpenAI's internal agent monitoring. One gap they found, now patched, was that monitoring only triggered when an agent handed control back to the user, leaving around ten per cent of internal Codex traffic unmonitored between May and July. Via T L D R and The Rundown A I.
Now, over to start-ups and venture.
Section three, start-ups and venture.
First, Sifted's analysis of Nvidia's European spending spree, which wrapped up with its Berlin event after investments in Paris, London, Stockholm and Berlin. The pattern mirrors the United States: Nvidia mostly backs companies that buy its chips, chiefly compute buyers and A I cloud builders. Investors are mixed on whether that is healthy for the ecosystem. Via Sifted.
Second, the gap between Nordic capitals. Stockholm start-ups have raised four and a half billion euros so far this year, more than double last year, while Oslo has raised just two hundred and seventeen million. Local investors blame thin growth capital and a culture where the dream is a quick sale, though they see an edge in industrial and physical A I. A useful reminder that ecosystems are made at the growth stage, not the seed stage. Via Sifted.
Third, fresh money in European venture. Madrid's Seaya Nova has raised six hundred million euros for a growth fund and is opening in London, and the median Italian early-stage round this year is one point eight million euros, up from one million in twenty twenty four. Via Sifted.
Now, over to policy and geopolitics.
Section four, policy and geopolitics.
First, the White House has opened trade negotiations on wind turbine imports, about seventy eight per cent of which are made in China, under its national security investigation powers. That could mean more tariffs. Via International Intrigue.
Second, Brazil goes to a presidential runoff on Sunday, and polling puts Lula and Bolsonaro neck and neck. Bond markets have noticed: ten year yields ticked back up this week as traders reprice the chance of a spendier incumbent staying in power. Via International Intrigue.
Third, Germany's chancellor says the country faces intense espionage after the arrest of a Ukrainian national accused of passing military secrets, including on tank production and NATO's eastern flank, to Russia. As Germany rearms, it widens the surface for approaches. Via International Intrigue.
Now, over to community, events and marketing.
Section five, community, events and marketing. One idea worth stealing.
From Priya Parker, the Magical Question. At a family dinner spanning a seventy eight year old and three children, she asked everyone one thing: what is something specific your mum or dad did for you as a child that made you feel really loved? A good question, she says, is one everyone wants to answer and wants to hear others answer. This one worked because it put every age on equal footing as a child, and it opened stories nobody had told before. The takeaway: for your next event, dinner or community call, replace the round of introductions with one question like this, and write it down in advance. Via Priya Parker.
Finally, section six, one interesting thing.
From Marginal Revolution, a paper on how long wealth shocks last. Looking at England from seventeen hundred to today, the authors find that a windfall or a loss fades in under three generations. It cuts against the idea that fortunes today are mostly explained by events before nineteen hundred, and suggests that families regress to the average faster than we assume. Via Marginal Revolution.
That's Byte-sized for today. Thanks for listening, and see you tomorrow.

item.title: Byte-sized — Friday, 23 October
item.description:
Good morning, and welcome to Byte-sized for Friday, the twenty third of October. Six sections today, and we begin, as ever, in Japan and the Asia Pacific.
Section one, Japan and Asia Pacific.
First, a social app that is booming in Japan and South Korea. Setlog is less than a year old and already has around ten million users. It prompts you to record a two second clip every hour, then stitches the day into a short day in the life video that you share only with chosen groups of friends. No editing is allowed, so what people see is your actual day, not your highlight reel. Scan Club reads it as a sign that online social life keeps shrinking from public feeds towards small, trusted circles, and a reminder to look beyond North America for what might arrive next. Via Scan Club.
Second, the C S I S Japan Chair has rounded up its recent work. The themes are telling: how Japanese elite opinion is shifting on nuclear weapons, what Prime Minister Takaichi's approval ratings mean for her second year in office, the implications of Japan's new national intelligence bureau, food security with a fresh look at rice, and the potential for American and Japanese cooperation in creative industries. It also highlights discussions on Japan as a maritime power facing China. If you are talking to government people about Japan, those are the live conversations. Via C S I S.
Now, over to AI and tech.
Section two, AI and tech.
First, the story of the week for anyone who runs a website. Two critical flaws in P H P, the language behind roughly seventy per cent of the web, were found with help from an OpenAI model, and patches have now been pushed. The bugs are around a decade old and let attackers take over servers without logging in. The American National Security Agency has urged anyone who cannot patch immediately to take systems offline, and government sites in Finland, Germany and the Netherlands did just that. Cloudflare says early attacks are emerging, and OpenAI says more significant finds are still being fixed. The lesson: old code is more fragile than anyone assumed, and AI is now finding the holes faster than people can. Via The Rundown A I and T L D R.
Second, Anthropic has launched Claude Duet, a personal agent app that can act on your behalf around the clock, even when your devices are off. It carries over memory and connectors from Claude, and can check out through Shop Pay and Stripe's Link using one time virtual cards. Anything involving deleting, paying or sending a message needs your sign off first. It is rolling out in waves to waitlisted American Pro and Max subscribers. Via The Rundown A I.
Third, OpenAI has acquired Orchestra Bio, a platform that helps biopharma teams coordinate drug development, and will fold it into its life sciences effort to build agents that connect scientific discoveries to clinical studies and regulatory work. Separately, OpenAI is selling its models and Codex through Google Cloud. Via T L D R and The Rundown A I.
Fourth, a quick one for software teams. Blacksmith, a continuous integration platform, hit a one billion dollar valuation after a sixty six million dollar round led by Sequoia, just two months after its previous raise. Its revenue has grown seventeen fold as A I coding agents generate more code that needs building and testing. Via T L D R.
Now, over to start-ups and venture.
Section three, start-ups and venture.
First, fintech funding is concentrating. Globally it fell twenty one per cent year on year to ten point six billion dollars in the third quarter, while deal count dropped thirty one per cent to its lowest level since at least twenty eighteen. Investors are favouring payments, stablecoin rails and agentic commerce, and asking everyone else for proof of durable demand. In that climate, Ramp, fresh from raising one point eight five billion dollars at a sixty billion dollar valuation, has applied for a national trust bank charter in the United States. Via T L D R.
Second, Europe keeps minting big rounds. Legal A I company Legora raised five hundred and fifty million dollars at an eight point eight billion dollar valuation, and the finance planning firm Pigment raised two hundred and fifty million in a Series E led by the European Union's Scaleup Europe Fund. Also, Yann LeCun and Mistral's Arthur Mensch backed Enact Intelligence's thirty million dollar pre seed, said to be Switzerland's largest. Via Sifted.
Third, Salesforce has agreed to buy the customer engagement platform Braze for about five point six six billion dollars in cash, and Braze shares jumped more than fifty per cent. Via T L D R.
Now, over to policy and geopolitics.
Section four, policy and geopolitics.
First, Britain's competition regulator has proposed much lower fees and fewer technical restrictions for companies that want to use the iPhone's contactless payment technology, a direct attempt to loosen Apple's grip on tap to pay. Via T L D R.
Second, big banks are now industrial policy players. JPMorgan says it has invested five billion dollars of its own equity in companies tied to American national security, across advanced manufacturing, energy, supply chains and defence technology, on top of around two hundred and thirty billion dollars financed through its wider initiative. Expect more of this kind of private capital lining up behind government priorities. Via T L D R.
Now, over to community, events and marketing.
Section five, community, events and marketing. Two ideas worth stealing.
First, from Scan Club, the unusual power of a pinned post. A court has ordered an influencer to pin a public apology to the top of her feeds for three and a half years after losing a defamation case. Whatever you think of the case, it shows how valuable that top slot is, and how it can be both an asset and a liability. The takeaway: treat whatever sits first on your page, your community space or your event site as your most valuable real estate, and choose it deliberately. Via Scan Club.
Second, from Skift, a lesson in community resilience. Attendees of the Grace Hopper Celebration, an event that was cancelled, are rallying to create new programmes of their own. When an official gathering disappears, the community can still build one. One idea worth stealing: keep a small group of members who could run the event without you. Via Skift.
Finally, section six, one interesting thing.
From Why Is This Interesting, a Japanese car with a lesson in restraint. Toyota's Century, first built in nineteen sixty seven, is a limousine favoured by Japan's boardrooms, ministries and the Imperial household. It is now a standalone brand and, from twenty twenty eight, will be sold in America through a small group of Lexus dealers. The current model is hand finished, with a phoenix badge that takes six weeks to carve and black paint sanded by hand three times. The writer's point is that the product is the absence of friction, and that Toyota is attempting something rare: to export restraint at a serious premium.
That's Byte-sized for today. Thanks for listening, and see you tomorrow.

item.title: Byte-sized — Thursday, 22 October
item.description:
Good morning, and welcome to Byte-sized for Thursday, the twenty second of October. Six sections today, and we begin, as ever, in Japan and the Asia Pacific.
Section one, Japan and Asia Pacific.
First, a warning light for Japanese industry. International Intrigue reports that Japan may have only months, not years, before it runs out of yttrium, a rare earth found in jet engines, semiconductors, electric vehicles and L E D lighting. China imposed export controls on the mineral last year, after Prime Minister Takaichi suggested Japan might respond in any war over Taiwan. Tokyo is now lobbying its American allies for help. For anyone selling into Japanese manufacturing, supply chain resilience has just become a boardroom topic. Via International Intrigue.
Second, China's economy is sending mixed signals. Third quarter growth accelerated to four point five per cent, up from four point three, which puts the five per cent target within reach. But retail sales are crawling at one per cent, and property investment has fallen another twenty per cent this year. The growth is coming from state funded high tech manufacturing, and high tech and industrial goods made up sixty four per cent of record new exports. In other words, Beijing is replacing weak confidence at home with subsidised demand abroad. Alongside that, the party has confirmed an investigation into Huang Qifan, the seventy four year old former mayor of Chongqing and an outspoken critic of the property sector, just before a major party plenum next week. Via International Intrigue.
Third, a trade deal fourteen years in the making. Switzerland's president has visited Vietnam to celebrate a free trade agreement between Vietnam and the European Free Trade Association, which covers Switzerland, Norway, Iceland and Liechtenstein. Vietnam gains high tech European investment, and the European bloc gains a foothold in South East Asia's manufacturing hub, as both sides diversify away from China and tariff uncertainty. Via International Intrigue.
Fourth, Accenture has reportedly hired J P Morgan to explore selling its Greater China consulting business, in a deal that could be worth up to one and a half billion dollars. A notable signal on how global professional services firms are rethinking their exposure to the region. Via T L D R.
Now, over to AI and tech.
Section two, AI and tech.
First, Sam Altman has reportedly described three possible endgames for AI safety to OpenAI staff. The one he favoured is a global watchdog modelled on the International Atomic Energy Agency. The second would merge the leading labs into one, in the style of CERN. The third, one lab racing ahead with self improving AI to, in his words, melt everyone else's chips, he called terrible. OpenAI reportedly has a year to pick a path, and Altman said it must include a speed limit for self improving systems. Via The Rundown AI.
Second, Microsoft has taken the unusual step of describing A I agents as akin to insider threats, saying frontier models cannot be trusted because they are unpredictable and lack organisational norms. Its answer is new Guardian Agents and agent detection in Defender, built on a principle worth remembering: separate the supply of intelligence from the authority over it. Separately, Microsoft has finished pretraining its own very large model, which suggests it is reducing its reliance on OpenAI. Via T L D R.
Third, a start-up with a manufacturing flavour. Bob McGrew, the former chief research officer at OpenAI, has launched Arda at a one point five billion dollar valuation after a one hundred and sixty million dollar round. It uses A I to help factories set up assembly lines for new products, and the defence firm Anduril says basic assembly instructions now take fifteen minutes instead of ten hours. McGrew's stated ambition is a fully automated Shenzhen in West Texas. Via The Rundown AI.
Fourth, the chip wars. Amazon has released TorchNeuron, which lets developers run PyTorch code on its Trainium chips with a simple configuration change, and plans to contribute code so the framework depends less on Nvidia's software. In China, DeepSeek has released the code for the engine behind its latest model, with support for Huawei chips, so firms can serve it without Nvidia hardware. Both are attacks on the same lock in. Via T L D R.
Now, over to start-ups and venture.
Section three, start-ups and venture.
First, Europe's Nvidia moment continues. Nvidia has announced investments in four German start-ups, adding to a European spending spree. Sifted also reports that Tallinn's cybersecurity company Blackwall raised one hundred million dollars in a Series C led by A V P. Via Sifted.
Second, fintech and foundation models. Sifted's fintech newsletter looks at transactional foundation models, A I systems trained on billions of payment events to speed up lending and fraud decisions. Revolut, with eighty million customers, is moving from idea to product in two to eight weeks and wants to get that down to days. One founder's view: the real barrier to entry is scale, even though Revolut helped publish the blueprint that rivals now follow. Via Sifted.
Third, Otter, the meeting transcription company, has secured three hundred and twenty million dollars of growth financing from General Catalyst, to turn meeting conversations into connected company knowledge. It reports more than forty million users. Via T L D R.
Now, over to policy and geopolitics.
Section four, policy and geopolitics.
First, energy is steering diplomacy. President Macron has toured the Gulf seeking fuel commitments, and Paris claims pledges equal to around ten per cent of French diesel use, offering advanced defence equipment in return. Meanwhile Secretary of State Rubio is in Uzbekistan with around two hundred American business leaders to court Central Asia on critical minerals and energy, before visiting Mumbai and Jamnagar. The aim is to give the region more options and make Beijing spend energy competing across Eurasia. Via International Intrigue.
Second, the European Union has unveiled its first Arctic strategy, promising undersea cable surveillance, more satellite capability and a new fleet of icebreakers, as Russia, China and the United States compete in the High North. Cable cuts and G P S jamming have pushed Brussels to treat the region as a security issue, not just an environmental one. Via International Intrigue.
Third, Ukraine's connectivity. Kyiv says American intelligence sharing has resumed after a brief freeze, while Washington denies any pause, and the White House and Elon Musk are still trading denials over who curbed Ukraine's Starlink access. Worth watching ahead of the American midterms. Via International Intrigue.
Now, over to community, events and marketing.
Section five, community, events and marketing. Two ideas worth stealing.
First, from Skift, a fix for awkward networking. After the I M E X trade show in Las Vegas, the writer suggests small adjustments that make events feel like a conversation with a new friend, not a chore, and notes that it doesn't have to involve alcohol. The takeaway for any organiser: design low pressure ways to start conversations, instead of leaving people with a lanyard, a drink and a crowded room. Via Skift.
Second, a negotiating tip for anyone booking venues. Wall Street expects American hotel revenue growth to slow in twenty twenty seven, partly because next summer is measured against this year's World Cup crowds. Revenue managers are judged year on year, so a group filling soft nights helps them. The advice is to ask for more than you would have last year, such as a better rate or friendlier terms. Via Skift.
Finally, section six, one interesting thing.
In Uncharted Territories, Tomas Pueyo argues that most intelligence is really search. Writing, printing and the internet each made it cheaper to find other people's ideas, and large language models have now pushed that cost close to zero. So where does the human edge lie? His answer is the query: noticing problems nobody has searched for, combining fields in new ways, and working where data does not exist, in unrecorded things such as noticing what people need before they say so. If intelligence is search, your edge is the question you ask.
That's Byte-sized for today. Thanks for listening, and see you tomorrow.

item.title: Byte-sized — Tuesday, 20 October
item.description:
Good morning, and welcome to Byte-sized for Tuesday, the twentieth of October. Six sections today, and we begin, as ever, in Japan and the Asia Pacific.
Section one, Japan and Asia Pacific.
First, Japan is going to Mars, or at least to its moons. The Japanese space agency, JAXA, is set to launch its Martian Moons eXploration mission around now, aiming to reach Phobos, collect a sample from the surface, and bring it back to Earth by twenty thirty one. The mission leans on American, French and German technology for parts of the build, which makes it a quiet showcase for Tokyo's role as a trusted partner in the deep space race. It also tests whether Phobos could serve as a low gravity staging post for future journeys to Mars. Via International Intrigue.
Second, a number that says a lot about the media business. For the first time since the Japan Press Research Institute began its survey in two thousand and eight, fewer than half of people in Japan, forty nine point eight per cent, now pay for a monthly newspaper subscription. For anyone building or investing in media, content or subscription products in Japan, the traditional habit is clearly weakening. Via International Intrigue.
Third, a follow-up on the Asian chip story we covered yesterday. China's memory maker CXMT now expects a nine month net profit of around nineteen point seven billion US dollars, against a small loss a year earlier, with revenue jumping from roughly four and a half billion dollars to nearly thirty eight billion. The company credits AI driven shortages of memory chips and expanded capacity. Two cautions: the claim that it has fifth generation memory in mass production has not been independently verified, and memory booms have a habit of ending when new capacity floods the market. Still, it explains why Japanese and Korean equipment makers are nervous. Via T L D R.
Now, over to AI and tech.
Section two, AI and tech.
First, Microsoft reportedly plans to pay Anthropic more than two billion dollars a year to use Claude models inside its Copilot assistant. The reason appears to be performance pressure from customers on tasks such as financial automation and presentations. Microsoft is also running an internal router that sends some workloads to OpenAI models, so this looks less like a switch and more like a portfolio approach to suppliers. Via T L D R.
Second, Anthropic has announced a Public Benefit Fund, a company owned entity that would receive five per cent of its equity if shareholders agree, with more added as the company's value climbs. The fund could support nonprofits or make direct payments to groups affected by AI, such as displaced workers, with no money going to lobbying or politics. Together with founder and employee pledges, the company says about a fifth of its equity is now set aside for public benefit. The Rundown notes that until money actually reaches people, it will be hard to tell this apart from good public relations. Via The Rundown AI.
Third, the same company has published research on its own workforce, and the findings are striking. By August, hours worked by employees' AI agents outnumbered the hours of the humans by six to one. Junior staff fell from twenty seven per cent of technical hires to just nine per cent, and engineers are shipping about five times as many code changes as six months ago. Agents sit idle roughly eighty per cent of the time waiting for a person to respond, so human attention has become the bottleneck. Via The Rundown AI.
Fourth, in hardware, Intel and Qualcomm are reportedly bidding up to ten billion dollars for the chip start-up Tenstorrent. Its chips cost around a thousand dollars and run a compact number format natively, where GPUs with native support list near forty thousand. Those cost figures come from vendors and are unverified, and no deal has closed, but it shows how hard the big chip makers are chasing alternatives to Nvidia. Via T L D R.
Now, over to start-ups and venture.
Section three, start-ups and venture.
First, the payments firm Ramp has raised one point eight five billion dollars at a sixty billion dollar valuation, up from forty four billion only four months ago. Annualised revenue has passed two billion dollars, and it is moving beyond expense management into payments, accounting, procurement and AI infrastructure, including cards designed for AI agents. Via T L D R.
Second, agents buying things is becoming real. Stripe's president says agent driven commerce on its platform went vertical in September, helped by agents that can now use ordinary websites without special integrations. American Express has promised to cover cardholder losses when a registered agent makes a purchase error, though the fine print matters, and Mercury now lets agents prepare payments, with a human approving the final transfer. Liability and authorisation are the open questions to watch. Via T L D R.
Third, Europe. Nvidia's Jensen Huang has been touring Paris and London, teasing around two billion dollars in new European investments, including French firms Doctolib and Pigment and five British start-ups. Nvidia says it has put eight billion dollars into European start-ups in the past year. Sifted also reports that Accel is set to lead a sixty million dollar round for Revolution Labs, founded by the former DeepMind researcher Nando de Freitas. Via Sifted.
Now, over to policy and geopolitics.
Section four, policy and geopolitics.
First, a possible summit with Asia at its centre. International Intrigue reports that Vladimir Putin has proposed a meeting with Donald Trump and Xi Jinping on the sidelines of the APEC summit in Shenzhen, on the eighteenth and nineteenth of November, to discuss ending the war in Ukraine, with Ukraine not invited. The newsletter's reading is that Xi may enjoy the role of mediator but is also comfortable with a distracted America. Meanwhile, Trump quietly exempted Russia from new sanctions late on Friday, saying it was to protect peace talks. Worth knowing before any conversation about Asia Pacific diplomacy. Via International Intrigue.
Second, the United Kingdom is drawing up plans for mandatory safety reporting by frontier AI companies, as the government seeks more oversight of powerful models. Alongside that, Sifted looks at Europe's enthusiasm for open weight models as a route to sovereignty, and the risk that safety guardrails can be stripped out. Supporters argue openness is an accountability guarantee, since anyone can inspect and test the models. Via Sifted.
Third, a practical point for founders: Sifted asks why governments are so hard to sell to. Procurement can leave fast-moving start-ups waiting years for contracts, and Britain's Sovereign AI Fund is trying to make the state an easier customer. Via Sifted.
Now, over to community, events and marketing.
Section five, community, events and marketing. One idea worth stealing.
The community platform company Bevy's C M X network is running a circuit tour of small in-person meetups, and nearly one hundred community professionals have joined across its first six stops this autumn. The formats are modest and easy to copy: a casual morning of coffee and a neighbourhood walk in Los Angeles, a brewery evening with shuffleboard in Boston, and pizza and practical conversation in Nashville. The lesson is to launch a chapter city by city with a relaxed, low cost format rather than a big conference. Also, nominations for its community awards close on the twentieth of November. Via C M X Newsletter.
Finally, section six, one interesting thing.
In Why Is This Interesting's Monday media diet, the hotelier Marc Blazer shares an idea from the philosopher Bernard Suits. Play, in Suits' words, is voluntarily taking on unnecessary obstacles in order to enjoy overcoming them. Blazer's point is that we spend so much effort removing friction from life that we forget many of our greatest joys come from it, which is why he restores old cars rather than buying a new one. Via Why Is This Interesting.
That's Byte-sized for today. Thanks for listening, and see you tomorrow.

item.title: Byte-sized — Monday, 19 October
item.description:
Good morning, and welcome to Byte-sized for Monday, the nineteenth of October. Six sections today, and we begin, as ever, in Japan and the Asia Pacific.
Section one, Japan and Asia Pacific.
First, a rough week for the chip makers of East Asia. Tokyo Electron, Japan's chipmaking equipment giant, fell seven point two per cent in a single day. The trigger was news that China's memory underdog, CXMT, has made progress on a new type of high density memory chip and has now captured around ten per cent of the global market. That leaves Japanese and Korean hardware firms feeling sandwiched between squeezed Western buyers on one side and rising Chinese suppliers on the other. SoftBank also dropped about nine per cent on its wider exposure to artificial intelligence investments. For balance, Tokyo Electron is still up around forty per cent this year. Via International Intrigue.
Second, Indonesia. The index provider MSCI says it is considering moving Indonesia's stock market from emerging to standalone status, which would remove it from the main global indices. Jakarta's benchmark fell eleven per cent in one day, its worst in decades, and is down forty per cent since January. MSCI points to opaque ownership, concentrated insider holdings and weak enforcement, a heavy blow to a government that promised eight per cent growth on foreign investment. Via International Intrigue.
Third, Cambodia's scam centres, where Japan has a seat at the table. A CSIS commentary asks whether the clean up is working. Cambodia passed its first anti-scam law in April, says it has shut more than two hundred centres, and has released some two hundred thousand people. It declared victory in August. But Amnesty International reports that more than seventy per cent of the compounds it identified appear to have been ignored, and that some were warned in advance and moved. Scams are estimated to make up between forty and sixty per cent of the country's economy, which is why elite networks are so hard to touch. September's Phnom Penh Declaration was backed by the United States, China, Japan and every ASEAN state except Thailand. The test now is whether the elites behind the compounds are ever investigated. Via CSIS.
Fourth, a number from CSIS to keep in your pocket: North Korea's overseas labour programme now covers more than one hundred thousand workers in at least seventeen countries, earning the state between four hundred and fifty and eight hundred million dollars a year. And Intrigue notes that the long delayed New Yalu River Bridge between North Korea and China has finally opened, after twelve years. Via CSIS and International Intrigue.
Now, over to artificial intelligence and technology.
Section two, AI and tech.
First, who is actually paying for AI. Ramp's October index finds that just one per cent of firms account for eighty per cent of spending on OpenAI and Anthropic. September spending per employee was three point one per cent below its July peak, even as total token volumes rose, and the index suggests falling model prices are the reason. A related note: five frontier models now score within five points of each other on one intelligence benchmark, yet the cost of finishing the same tasks differs by three point eight times. The practical lesson is to test your own real requests across candidate models before choosing a default. Via TLDR.
Second, ASML cannot keep up. It sold one hundred and thirteen lithography systems in the third quarter, up from eighty six, for record sales of eleven point seven billion euros. It now expects supply in both 2027 and 2028 to fall short of demand, even after a planned thirty per cent capacity boost, and some customers want to place orders for 2029 and 2030. Via TLDR.
Third, the other side of the boom: debt. Intrigue walks through a tech sell-off. CoreWeave, the rental landlord of AI computing power, has borrowed around fifty billion dollars, and bonds it issued in June at nine point six per cent are now being priced to yield fifteen. Oracle fell nine per cent in a day. The International Monetary Fund notes that AI hyperscalers now issue ten per cent of all new investment grade corporate bonds, up from one per cent two years ago. Yet TSMC posted a record quarterly profit of twenty three point six billion dollars. The old gold rush line applies: the seller of pickaxes tends to be the last to suffer. Via International Intrigue.
Fourth, travel meets agents. Booking Holdings has launched Vayo, an AI travel agent that organises bookings from a user's inbox and watches trips for savings and disruption, including reservations made outside Booking's own brands. The company plans to invest one hundred million dollars. Via PhocusWire.
Now, over to startups and venture.
Section three, startups and venture.
First, cybersecurity funding. Crunchbase counts six point eight billion dollars invested in the third quarter, up fifty per cent on the previous quarter and driven by larger rounds. Keyfactor raised one billion, Cyera four hundred million, and Visa agreed to buy BioCatch for two point four billion. Via TLDR.
Second, a warning for investors in defence technology. Sifted reports that European investors see fuzzy revenue reporting in the sector, with confusion between bookings and recognised revenue. One investor was shown revenue that came from a veterans' association, and another is often shown grant funding presented as defence sales. Classified contracts make checking harder still. The advice from one investor: accounting is accounting. Via Sifted.
Third, state money for deep tech. The British Business Bank has put one hundred and eighty million pounds into six AI and deep tech venture funds, including Entrepreneurs First. Its chief investment officer says the country's funding landscape does not match its technical excellence. Meanwhile Nvidia has spoken of two billion dollars of new investment across Europe. Via Sifted.
Now, over to policy and geopolitics.
Section four, policy and geopolitics.
Two items worth having ready for conversations with government or enterprise people. First, the United States has proposed four hundred and twenty nine million dollars for conventional bunker busting weapons in its next defence budget, against an average of one hundred and twenty three million over the past ten years, as stocks of weapons for deeply buried targets run thin, according to CSIS. Second, Ukraine says SpaceX has capped the speed of military satellite terminals mounted on drones, with no warning, causing missions to be cancelled. Officials suspect it is deliberate, and a Ukrainian firm is developing an alternative. It is a vivid reminder of what depending on a private provider means. Via CSIS and TLDR.
Third, the Pacific. New Zealand is sending a six month team to help Fiji overhaul its security agencies, after Washington warned that China linked hackers had gained access to a regional organisation based in Suva. The United States has not named the target, though speculation points to the Pacific Islands Forum secretariat, which denies it. Intrigue reads it as Washington stepping up counter intelligence in a region where Beijing and Taipei are competing for recognition, and where Japan is also an active partner. Via International Intrigue.
Now, over to community, events and marketing.
Section five, one idea worth stealing.
From Priya Parker, a tool for community builders. Before you react to a group conflict, ask what kind of fight it is. She plots two things: how intense it is, and how much it touches the question of who we are as a group. Low on both is a kerfuffle. High intensity but low identity is a brawl. Quiet but existential is a hairline fracture. Loud and existential is a rift. Her example is a lesbian bar in Massachusetts that dropped its mask rule on Saturday nights to raise revenue. The owners saw a business decision, but members saw a betrayal of the bar's purpose. Spot the identity question early and you can answer it properly.
And one for marketers, from a TLDR piece on the app Cal AI. It paid fitness creators thousands of dollars to post and saw no spike in downloads, because viewers were not the right audience. It now reads the comments for people asking for help the app provides, and caps what it pays per thousand views at what those views earn. Check the comments for customers before paying for reach. Via TLDR.
Now, one last thing.
Section six, one interesting thing. Works in Progress, by Charles Mann, asks what on earth is Dekton, the new surface on his induction cooktop. The answer is porcelain. It is one of humanity's oldest high technologies, first made over three thousand years ago in China, and one of its newest. Europeans spent centuries failing to copy it, until an alchemist locked in a fortress attic and a mathematician finally got there in seventeen oh eight. Today, a slab pressed under twenty five thousand tonnes is nearly unbreakable, and porcelain scaffolds are even used to grow replacement bone. His son has never known a world that was not made of porcelain. Via Works in Progress.
That's Byte-sized for today. Thanks for listening, and see you tomorrow.

item.title: Byte-sized — Friday, 16 October
item.description:
Good morning, and welcome to Byte-sized for Friday, the sixteenth of October. Five sections today, and we begin, as ever, in Japan and the Asia Pacific.
Section one, Japan and Asia Pacific.
One for your diary in Fukuoka. Fukuoka Now is holding Kyushu Roundtable number seven, titled Fukuoka's Next Chapter, at CIC Fukuoka in Tenjin on Friday the thirtieth of October. With the mayoral election approaching, the evening asks what the city should prioritise over the next four years. An architect, Kyoko Matsuoka, and Evan Kirby, who founded a Japanese language and culture school, will open the discussion, with plenty of room for audience questions. It runs in English, is free, and places are limited, with applications reviewed before acceptance. Via Fukuoka Now.
Now, over to artificial intelligence and technology.
Section two, AI and tech.
First, Anthropic has outgrown Git. With AI generated code pushing roughly thirty thousand merged changes a day, the company built its own version control system, called Scion, and moved its main code repository across in five months. It assumes engineers are always online, uses a central server with server side commits, and cut processor and memory needs by around two hundred times, while code checkouts for testing dropped from minutes to seconds. The wider point: when writing code gets cheap, the tooling around it becomes the bottleneck. Via TLDR.
Second, Nvidia in Britain. At an event in London, Jensen Huang announced minority stakes in five UK companies, spanning molecular modelling, infrastructure planning, automated discovery, quantum error correction and biological models. He also told the room that Britain tends to find the one reason not to win, out of a million ways to do it. Via Sifted.
Third, the shopping agents arrive. Shopify is opening its catalogue to personal shopping agents, and to tools such as ChatGPT, Copilot and Gemini, while keeping a human sign off on every purchase. Meanwhile JPMorgan is blocking outside AI agents from moving customers' money directly, citing security and liability, while building its own tools. Two of the biggest commerce gatekeepers are drawing the line in different places, and that line is where the next fights will be. Via TLDR.
Now, over to startups and venture.
Section three, startups and venture.
First, Sifted's second AI one hundred ranking of Europe's most promising AI startups. Stockholm's Tandem Health, an assistant for clinicians used in fourteen countries, tops the list. Half the companies are vertical specialists, fourteen apply AI to the physical world, and thirteen of last year's list have since become unicorns. Y Combinator is on the cap table of thirteen of this year's hundred. Via Sifted.
Second, a take private to watch. Bumble is reportedly in advanced talks to be bought by Ithaca Holdings at about one billion dollars, well above its market value of three hundred and eighty nine million before the report, as paying users and younger audiences drift away. Via TLDR.
Third, a pricing puzzle. Monzo, valued at five point nine billion dollars, trades at about three times revenue, while Revolut's latest share sale values it near nineteen times revenue. Same sector, very different multiples. Via TLDR.
Now, over to policy and geopolitics.
Section four, policy and geopolitics.
A study commissioned by a United States technology industry group says European cloud sovereignty rules could cost the continent one hundred and fifteen billion euros over a decade. Treat the number carefully, since it is a modelled scenario from an interested party, but expect it to feature in Brussels debates about digital independence, and in any conversation with enterprise buyers weighing where to host their data. Via TLDR.
Now, over to community, events and marketing.
Section five, one idea worth stealing.
From Fukuoka Now, the format itself. Their roundtable is timed to a live local issue, the mayoral election, and opens with one simple question: what is one thing you would change? Two short openers, a moderator, a reception beforehand, and room for the audience. If you run events, topical timing and a single easy question beat a long programme. And a second, from Skift's meetings desk: Timeleft charges nineteen ninety nine a month to seat strangers at dinner, and keeps names private until the night, with conversation prompts built in. Design the introduction, not just the venue. Via Skift.
Now, one last thing.
Section six, one interesting thing. Why Is This Interesting looks at bibliotherapy, a word coined in nineteen sixteen. In the First World War, librarians wheeled book carts into military hospitals, and one British scholar drew up a fever chart of prescribed reading. For soldiers with shell shock, one prescription was Jane Austen: not a book explaining trauma, but a story about the ordinary complications of being human. The suggestion is that information is not the same as consolation. Via Why Is This Interesting.
That's Byte-sized for today. Thanks for listening, and see you tomorrow.
